Industry observers note that in two days, federal authorities filed suits against two states that treat prediction markets as illegal gambling. The cases could decide whether state gaming regulators or the CFTC control sports event contracts, which compete with licensed sportsbooks and online casinos.

The federal government has opened two fresh court fights with states over prediction markets. Both target state actions against event contracts offered on CFTC-regulated exchanges. Arkansas and Louisiana treat those contracts as illegal gambling. Washington argues that federal law takes priority.

Recent findings suggest that the Arkansas complaint carries case number 4:26-cv-01255-BSM. It is aimed at the enforcement action Griffin filed against KalshiEX LLC and Kalshi Inc. That state suit alleges multiple violations of the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act. It seeks restitution, penalties, taxes and injunctive relief.

In release 9325-26, the CFTC remarked Arkansas could seek civil penalties against CFTC-registered exchanges that could reach hundreds of millions of dollars. The federal suit also aims to stop the state from halting event-contract trading. The government wants a preliminary and permanent injunction. That order would bar Arkansas officials from investigating CFTC-regulated entities, their affiliates and partners. It would also stop them from enforcing state law against those firms over transactions on designated contract markets.

Griffin’s stance is not newly introduced. In October 2025, he issued a formal opinion that sports event contracts are gambling and require a license. The new case brings the preemption fight into the Eighth Circuit, which has not yet ruled on the question.

Sources indicate that with Arkansas added, the CFTC’s tally of state lawsuits over federal authority reaches 11. The agency has also filed amicus briefs in four federal appeals courts and one state supreme court.

Sources indicate that the Louisiana case moved within a day. Judge Jeffrey Johnson of the 21st Judicial District Court in Tangipahoa Parish signed the restraining order. The named entities are linked to Kalshi, Polymarket, Robinhood, Crypto.com, Coinbase, Gemini, ForecastEx, Novig, Underdog, IG Group and ProphetX.

According to recent reports, in release 9326-26, the CFTC stated the order shut down more than 30 companies tied to CFTC-regulated derivatives without giving them notice or a chance to be heard. The federal suit was filed in the Eastern District of Louisiana. It names the state, Attorney General Liz Murrill, the Louisiana Gaming Control Board and the state police gaming enforcement division. It asks the court to declare state gambling laws preempted. It also seeks to stop Louisiana from enforcing or extending the state order.

🚨Breaking: Louisiana judge orders temporary restraining order prohibiting Kalshi, Polymarket, Coinbase, Robinhood, and other “prediction market” operators from continuing their unlicensed and unregulated illegal gambling in Louisiana.

It’s not complicated: if you aren’t a… pic.twitter.com/gzrQlN9CCL.

— Attorney General Liz Murrill (@AGLizMurrill) November 12, 2026.

In a recent development, the exchange between officials has been sharp. CFTC Chairman Michael Selig described Louisiana’s emergency suit as “naked lawfare and a cynical political stunt.” On Nov. 14, Murrill answered on X. She accused Selig of “flatly false statements” and argued that states have regulated gambling for 250 years.

For licensed sportsbooks and online casinos, the outcome matters directly. If federal preemption holds, sports event contracts could operate outside state gaming rules in both states. The federal requests to block both states’ actions now go before the U.S. District Courts for the Eastern Districts of Arkansas and Louisiana.

#115613. Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1417 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Css-tricks ↗ Open Full Page

Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1417 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset.
  • I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.
  • In a recent development, use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset. text-wrap: pretty can prevent a stranded word, container query units can scale a heading to the column it occupies, and text-box can trim the half-leading built into a line box. Some of these features are experimental and browser support is uneven, so they need guardrails rather than blind inclusion.

I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.

In a recent development, use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you. I’ll walk you through all the details in this article and give you the full code at the end.

font-synthesis: none stops a browser from inventing bold or italic when the family lacks that face. The smoothing and text-rendering declarations are rendering hints, mainly for WebKit; results still vary by platform.

text-size-adjust disables mobile font inflation that can make a deliberately sized layout jump on rotation. font-size-adjust: from-font uses font metrics to reduce the apparent size change while a fallback swaps for a webfont.

(As with other snippets in this article, this ⁠:root block is a partial excerpt the final stylesheet combines it with additional custom properties defined later on.).

Viewport-based fluid type does not know how wide its element is. A heading in a narrow sidebar can therefore scale as though it fills the viewport.

container-type: inline-size makes the wrapper a container query, so its children can use cqi: a unit based on the container rather than the viewport. Replacing vw in clamp() lets the same heading scale appropriately in an article column or a 300px sidebar without component-specific media queries.

According to recent reports, line-height includes space above the cap-height and below the baseline: half-leading. It becomes obvious when text must align tightly with another element. text-box-trim removes it, while text-box-edge measures from capital-letter caps to the alphabetic baseline. This is a metrics-aware alternative to font-specific negative-margin nudges.

Selectors Level 5 proposes :heading, matching h1 to h6 and [role="heading"]. It has not landed in browsers, so keep it behind an @supports selector() check.

According to recent reports, default heading wrapping can leave one short final line. text-wrap: balance distributes text across its lines and works best for blocks of up to about six lines. For paragraphs, text-wrap: pretty avoids a stranded final word without balancing the whole block. Both replace JavaScript orphan fixers. Editable text needs text-wrap: stable, which prevents each upcoming word from reshuffling the paragraph.

hyphens: auto relies on the browser’s language dictionaries, so the document needs a correct lang attribute (for example ). Without one the browser has no dictionary to use and won’t be able to hyphenate text. Even with the correct lang, the defaults can leave tiny word fragments or several hyphenated lines in a row.

It has been revealed that hyphenate-limit-chars controls the smallest breakable word and fragments; hyphenate-limit-lines prevents a ladder effect. hyphenate-limit-zone makes breaks less frequent, while hyphenate-limit-last protects the final word. Safari needs the prefixed equivalents, so declare both sets together.

Set code, variables, and headings to hyphens: manual: a broken code word can change meaning, and a hyphenated heading usually reads as an error.

Punctuation marks don’t carry the same visual weight as letters, so a quotation mark sitting at the start of a line can look slightly indented against the text below it. hanging-punctuation lets specified punctuation sit fractionally outside the text block’s edge.

It has been revealed that the first value handles opening punctuation, and last handles closing punctuation at the end of a block, while allow-end lets punctuation hang past the right edge rather than force-wrapping. The result is a text block whose edges read as genuinely flush.

Underlines have a related problem. Browsers apply flat, one-size-fits-all thickness and position regardless of the font’s actual weight.

It has been revealed that text-decoration-thickness: from-font reads the thickness the font’s designer intended. text-underline-offset gives descenders room to breathe, and text-decoration-skip-ink: auto interrupts the underline wherever a descender crosses it rather than drawing straight through the letter.

Variable fonts often include an optical size axis, or opsz. It lets a typeface use thinner strokes at large display sizes and thicker, more legible strokes when set small.

font-optical-sizing: auto lets the font make that adjustment based on its actual rendered size. The @supports block covers the older font-variation-settings syntax some browsers still need, while font-variant-ligatures and font-kerning enable the font’s own ligatures and kerning pairs.

Light text on a dark background genuinely reads heavier than the same weight on a light background. Where a font ships a GRAD, or grade, axis, the dark mode block dials that perceived weight down without changing glyph shape or width the way an actual weight change would. Fonts without a GRAD axis safely ignore the setting.

In a recent development, mixing a monospace font into running prose often exposes a mismatched x-height at the same declared font-size. The size-adjust keyword, set once at the @font-face level, scales that font’s rendered output specifically, leaving the actual font-size value untouched.

Numbers in a table need identical widths so they stack into a clean column on the screen. Conversely, numbers in flowing text don’t need the same treatment and should sit naturally alongside the surrounding words.

In a recent development, the tabular-nums and lining-nums keywords give table digits a fixed width and full cap height. oldstyle-nums and proportional-nums let digits sit alongside lowercase letters without sticking up and disrupting the sentence’s texture.

font-variant-emoji makes the choice between full-colour and monochrome emoji explicit. Without it, the browser or platform gets to choose a fallback, and the result can vary more than you expect. Apply .emoji-color or .emoji-mono to containers where you want to enforce that choice, rather than setting it globally on the body.

Quote style and character order differ by language and region. English nests single quotes inside double quotes, British English reverses that convention, and French uses guillemets with a thin space.

In a recent development, the quotes property declares the order for each language through :lang(). The native q element then inserts the right pair through open-quote and close-quote. The same markup can render correctly in each locale without hardcoding characters into the content.

Wrapping the rules in :where() keeps them at zero specificity, so a project can override the quote style with one plain class.

In a recent development, default sub and sup styling is synthesized. The browser just shrinks the text and shifts the baseline, rather than using glyphs actually designed for that position.

According to recent reports, font-variant-position switches to the font’s own purpose-built sub and superscript glyphs where they exist, resetting vertical-align, font-size, and line-height so they don’t fight against the real glyph’s intended size and position. Most typefaces only include proper numerals rather than letters, so check the specific font before applying this broadly.

In a recent development, :where() always resolves to zero specificity, which is useful for a reset. Every rule here is an opinionated default, and wrapping it in :where() lets a project override a property with a plain class.

It has been revealed that :is() solves a different problem: repetition. The heading selector list appears several times in a typographic stylesheet, and grouping it avoids the risk of forgetting a level.

Unlike :where(), :is() carries the specificity of its most specific argument.

Here’s the complete reset, combining the stable layers. Unsupported declarations are ignored by the browser, so the stylesheet can be adopted gradually.

Recent findings suggest that much of this CSS removes work that used to leak into other parts of a build. text-wrap can take over orphan handling from JavaScript, container query units keep a component’s type scale tied to its own width, and text-box-trim avoids the negative margins once used to compensate for leading. quotes, font-variant-position, and font-optical-sizing hand several smaller details back to the language and the font instead of a collection of one-off fixes.

Browser support will continue to change, especially for text-wrap and text-box-trim. Unsupported declarations are ignored, but that only helps when the unenhanced typography is acceptable in its own right.

Some of these rules are still too latest for a baseline reset. A news article, a marketing page, and an editable product interface do not ask the same things of their text; the set that belongs in yours depends on the font, the content, and the browsers you still need to support.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • According to recent reports, you can build an AI agent in an afternoon now.
  • Then it meets a real system with real permissions and real customers, and things get quiet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

According to recent reports, you can build an AI agent in an afternoon now. Pick a model, write a loop, hand it a few tools and watch it book a meeting or open a pull request. The demo works, and everyone in the room is impressed.

Then it meets a real system with real permissions and real customers, and things get quiet. Gartner has predicted that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, citing rising costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Its analyst Anushree Verma described most current projects as early-stage experiments that are driven by hype and often misapplied. A forecast is not a measurement, but the pattern it describes matches what many teams report: the agent is rarely what breaks. The workflow around it is.

This article covers where that workflow tends to fail, with a focus on permissions, tool connections and human approval. It includes a small, runnable policy gate in JavaScript, compares the main safeguards and notes their limits. Standards and guidance change swiftly in this area, so check the linked sources for the current versions.

A year or two ago the model was often the differentiator. Today many teams can reach the same frontier models through the same kinds of APIs, so if the intelligence is similar, the advantage has to come from somewhere else.

In a recent development, anthropic’s guide to building effective agents reached a similar conclusion after working with teams building agents. It reports that the most successful implementations were not using complex frameworks or specialized libraries, and were building with simple, composable patterns instead. It also separates workflows, where code paths are predefined, from agents, where the model chooses its own steps, and advises using the simplest approach that works and adding complexity only when measurement shows it helps.

Sources indicate that that should change where developers spend their time. Frameworks matter, but three less glamorous questions matter more: what can the agent touch, when does it stop, and who checks its work?

The OWASP guidance on Excessive Agency names what goes wrong here. It covers agents that can do more than they need to, and it traces the problem to three root causes: excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy.

In practice this looks familiar. An agent that only needs to read tickets is given a token that can also close them. A summarization tool connects with an admin account because that was quicker to set up. A generic “run shell command” tool is exposed when the agent only ever needs to write one file.

Sources indicate that the fix is ordinary engineering discipline applied to a fresh kind of caller. OWASP’s recommendations include giving each tool only the functions and permissions it needs, preferring narrow tools over open-ended ones, running actions under the user’s own scoped identity, requiring human approval for high-impact actions and enforcing authorization in the downstream system rather than letting the model decide. The last point is the vital one: a model can be talked out of a rule written in a prompt, but an API that checks scopes cannot.

Make the risky properties of a tool explicit in its definition so your orchestration layer can act on them:.

Nothing clever is happening there, which is the point. The decision about what needs a human is made by a developer at design time, not by a model at runtime.

The definitions above only help if something enforces them. The sketch below is a policy gate that sits between the model and your tools. It checks that the tool exists, that the caller was granted the scope, and whether the action is reversible, and it records each decision. It runs on Node.js 18 or later with no dependencies.

Sources indicate that A short test file highlights the behavior. Unknown tools and missing scopes are denied, reads run, and the irreversible send waits for a person:.

This is deliberately minimal. A real system would load scopes from the user’s actual session, enforce the same scopes again in the downstream API, and store the audit log somewhere durable. The gate is a second line of defense, not a replacement for authorization in the systems the agent calls.

The Model Context Protocol has become a common way to connect agents to tools. Anthropic donated MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation, in December 2025. Block contributed goose and OpenAI contributed AGENTS.md as founding projects, which shows how central the ecosystem has become.

According to recent reports, A standard protocol is good news. It also means you can install a tool server in minutes and expose every endpoint of your issue tracker, repository or CRM to your agent, whether it needs them or not. Easy connection quietly pushes more power to the agent.

Industry observers note that the protocol’s own security best practices document covers several relevant risks, including confused deputy problems in proxy servers, token passthrough, local server compromise and scope minimization. For scopes, it recommends starting with a minimal set and elevating only when a privileged operation is first attempted, and it lists wildcard or omnibus scopes as a common mistake.

A sensible rule is to treat every tool server like a third-party dependency running with production credentials. Review the tools it exposes, switch off the ones the workflow does not use, pin versions and log every call. If you would not let a latest contractor do it on day one, the agent should not do it either.

Industry observers note that human-in-the-loop design is often implemented as “approve everything”. That fails in a predictable way: people click approve forty times a day and stop reading by lunchtime.

A better rule is to gate on reversibility. Reads run freely, reversible writes run and get logged, and irreversible actions such as sending, paying or deleting wait for a person. Everything leaves a trace that a developer can replay when something looks odd. The gate above implements exactly this split.

Some teams build these pieces themselves, and others buy them. Elsewhen, a London-based consultancy that works on agentic operations for enterprise teams, describes its own service in similar terms. Its page lists approval gates where people sign off consequential decisions, an audit trail of what each agent read and which systems it touched, and a shared layer of permissions and guardrails that is reused across workflows. Elsewhen also states its Planet Agent report found that agents tend to start at the edges of an organization, where tasks are repeatable and mistakes are cheap, and then move toward the core. Treat that as the vendor’s own finding, and ask for the underlying evidence before relying on it.

Sources indicate that the same logic applies outside engineering. The first question worth asking any AI partner is what they have actually put into production, and developers can ask the same of their own work.

No single control is enough. The table summarizes what each safeguard does well and where it falls short.

It is the OWASP term for an agent that can do more than it needs to, caused by excessive functionality, permissions or autonomy.

A prompt rule can be bypassed or ignored, while a scope check in the downstream API is enforced regardless of what the model notes.

It has been revealed that usually not. Gating on reversibility keeps humans focused on actions such as sending, paying and deleting, and avoids approval fatigue.

Treat them like any third-party dependency. Review the tools they expose, limit scopes, pin versions and log calls.

The agentic projects that survive the next two years will probably not be the ones with the most ambitious autonomy. They will be the ones where someone sat down early and decided what the agent could touch, what it had to ask about and how anyone would know what it did.

That work does not demo well and it will not trend on social media. It is still the part that decides whether your agent becomes infrastructure or ends up among the projects that get cancelled.

  • It has been revealed that maine will become the eighth state with legal online casinos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that maine's Gambling Control Unit is heading toward an early 2027 launch of tribal-run online casinos after a single public hearing. A former lawmaker warns that the state's behavioral health system is too thin for a possible rise in gambling addiction, while a federal lawsuit still targets the tribes' exclusivity.

In a recent development, maine’s regulator is moving toward an early 2027 launch of tribal-run online casinos. Only one public hearing has been held so far. WGME’s I-Team reported on Nov. 16 that the Gambling Control Unit began iGaming rulemaking in June. Residents in the report raised a separate concern. They worry the state lacks the mental health and problem-gambling resources to cope.

It has been revealed that maine will become the eighth state with legal online casinos. Its four Wabanaki tribes hold exclusive licenses under LD 1164, the Wabanaki internet gaming act. The Legislature lists the measure as enacted as Public Law 538.

According to recent reports, the money set aside for addiction services is small next to the state’s cut. The legislative fiscal note sends 2% of adjusted gross iGaming receipts to the Gambling Addiction Prevention and Treatment Fund. The state’s own 18% share is projected at $1.8 million in fiscal 2025-26 and $3.6 million in fiscal 2026-27.

Sources indicate that critics doubt the system can absorb the demand. Patty Locuratolo Hymanson, a neurologist and former state lawmaker, told WGME that Maine lacks the behavioral health resources to handle a possible rise in gambling addiction from online casinos.

In a recent development, lawmakers reshaped the revenue split before passage. A committee amendment raised the state’s share from 16% to 18%. The same amendment cut the opioid treatment fund’s allocation from 3% to 1.5%. The fiscal note also carries ongoing General Fund appropriations of $645,354 for six Gambling Control Unit positions. Those include two criminal intelligence analysts and two auditors.

The regulator itself was skeptical at first. Before the bill became law, Executive Director Milt Champion opposed it in written testimony. He argued iGaming wasn’t warranted while sports wagering was only in its second year.

In a recent development, rulemaking is still underway. The unit issued its third version of the draft rules on Sept. 30, 2026, and took comments until Oct. 30. Champion has warned that major revisions would force a fourth publication. The third draft keeps the tax rate on adjusted gross receipts unchanged. It also retains the license fee and bond requirements. The regulator is hiring six staff members dedicated to iGaming.

Recent findings suggest that the launch also faces a court fight over tribal exclusivity. Churchill Downs and Oxford Casino Hotel brought their suit against the Gambling Control Unit and Champion in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maine. They are asking the court to declare the law unconstitutional. The challenge goes to the heart of the market’s design, which reserves online casino licenses for the tribes.

Recent findings suggest that the next deadlines are procedural. Under Maine’s rulemaking law, the unit has up to 120 days after comments close to adopt the rules. The Attorney General’s office has up to 150 days from that same date to approve them as legal. The unit’s rulemaking page also lists a public hearing notice marked Nov. 30, 2026, which could change that timetable.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that online casinos supplied most of the growth in Pennsylvania's October 2026 gaming revenue, while sports betting handle slipped.
  • Pennsylvania’s gaming revenue reached $634.4 million in October 2026, up 6.3% from a year earlier and the highest monthly total on record.
  • It has been revealed that iGaming accounted for about $27.7 million of the $37.4 million year-over-year increase.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that online casinos supplied most of the growth in Pennsylvania's October 2026 gaming revenue, while sports betting handle slipped. The results land as a stalled bill to ban sweepstakes casinos and raise sports betting taxes runs out of time.

Pennsylvania’s gaming revenue reached $634.4 million in October 2026, up 6.3% from a year earlier and the highest monthly total on record. Online casinos contributed a record $278.8 million, up 11.1%. The total cleared the previous single-month mark of $625.5 million, which was set in May 2026.

It has been revealed that iGaming accounted for about $27.7 million of the $37.4 million year-over-year increase. A year earlier, online casino revenue was $251,097,586, itself a record at the time. Total gaming tax revenue in October 2025 was $252,287,937, against a record $274 million this October.

Two licensees led the iGaming field. Hollywood Casino at Penn National generated $114.4 million, up 16%. Valley Forge Casino Resort followed with $75.2 million, up 5.3%.

In a recent development, october was a stronger month than September. In September, total gaming revenue was $555,036,870, a 4.07% year-over-year increase. iGaming table revenue slipped 0.63% that month.

Sources indicate that the October pattern mirrors the last fiscal year. iGaming revenue in fiscal 2025/26 was $2,933,453,989, an 18.42% gain over the prior year. It generated $1,337,414,660 in tax. Combined gaming revenue reached $7,005,987,435, an all-time fiscal-year high. Taxes and fees returned to the state totaled $3,098,193,583.

Industry observers note that pennsylvania’s online casino growth is in line with a slowing iGaming trend nationally. US iGaming revenue rose 12.3% year over year to $1.03 billion in August 2026. For the state budget, the vertical is now a central source of gaming tax.

Recent findings suggest that sports betting moved the other way on volume. Handle fell to $903 million from $968.5 million in October 2025. Revenue still rose, to $65.1 million from $60.7 million. The same split showed up across fiscal 2025/26. Handle dropped from $8,721,795,533 to $8,448,101,928. Sports wagering revenue rose 35.95% to $662,947,631.

Industry observers note that the record arrives as Harrisburg weighs a gaming modernization package. Rep. Russ Diamond introduced House Bill 2801 with four co-sponsors. On September 24, 2026, it was referred to the House Gaming Oversight Committee. Titled ‘Skill Games & Gaming Modernization,’ the bill would rewrite large parts of the state’s gaming code.

House Bill 2801 would make operating or promoting online sweepstakes games illegal in Pennsylvania. Fines would range from $50,000 to $500,000 per violation.

It has been revealed that the bill would also raise the sports wagering tax from 34% to 36%. The state currently taxes online slots at 54%. A higher sports rate would apply to a product whose handle is shrinking even as its revenue climbs.

The bill has not moved. HB 2801 had no recorded committee hearing or vote as of mid-November, according to Legal Sports Report. The legislative session ends November 30. Bills that do not pass by then do not carry into 2027.

Industry News: CSS-Tricks, Version 20

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2369 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I’ve been bashing on updating this site’s design for the last couple of weeks.
  • Sources indicate that it’s not like the site has simply sat all that time.
  • According to recent reports, now, before there’s a chorus of “things don’t look thaaaat different” I want to say I’m rarely a fan of complete re-builds and tend to lean into iterative releases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I’ve been bashing on updating this site’s design for the last couple of weeks. It’s high time things get a fresh coat of paint, right? The last version of CSS-Tricks was pushed five years ago. That’s ancient in web (and dog) years.

Sources indicate that it’s not like the site has simply sat all that time. We pushed lots of changes and shipped fresh features, particularly since 2024, but we never really got the paint brushes out of storage.

According to recent reports, now, before there’s a chorus of “things don’t look thaaaat different” I want to say I’m rarely a fan of complete re-builds and tend to lean into iterative releases. And the upcoming v20 theme is what I’d call an iterative rollup that’s worthy of a version bump.

Let’s go over the most notable updates to see why.

First and foremost, some of the biggest changes are what you don’t see. As you might imagine, this site has carried over plenty of pieces across 19 years. I decided to excavate the theme and definitely found some ghosts to bust.

Industry observers note that for example, the global compiled JavaScript file retained some scripts that just weren’t being used anymore. Things like handling embedded versions of the newsletter from before we began self-hosting the posts. There were relics that catered specifically to the Flexbox Guide for handling toggles back before we had proper HTML . There was a jQuery lazy-loader thing that is well-covered by WordPress core now. We had some scripts for serving third-party ads that are no longer needed now that we’re self-hosting ads. Things like that. The overall JavaScript was nicely trimmed from 151.6 KB (55.3 KB gzipped) to 133.8 KB (48.1 KB).

In a recent development, I also decided to formally retire the CSS-Tricks Forum. We put it in “archive mode” back in, like, 2018. None of those discussions are particularly valuable for today as they were over 10 years ago, so I deactivated the bbPress plugin that powered it and cleared out the database… and wow, that carved a whopping 400 MB from the ol’ database, not to mention it allowed me to drop several custom templates from the theme.

It has been revealed that there were more ghosts busted along the way and, to be sure, there are still some lurking around. But it’s way less scary poking around the theme directory now, and further cleanup should be a lot easier from here on out.

Yeah, yeah, raise your hand if you’re still running Gulp. We are 🙋‍♂️. That’s not a bad thing in and of itself, but keeping it in a fixed state for all this time is not the greatest. I think we’re sporting a more modern workflow than before, even if there’s still room to grow. A smattering of the related commits:.

Sources indicate that for years, I endured the same errors every time I fired up a fresh terminal. Those are gone and things run super cleanly, not to mention promptly. Very happy here.

Oof, this is everyone’s favorite job, right?! Aside from being able to spot and fix a few unescaped custom field calls here and there, I decided to ask Claude to help me with a holistic audit. I prompted it to review recent WordPress security release notes and identify areas where the theme could be hardened to comply with what WordPress is doing.

Industry observers note that whoa, you used AI? Yeah, I sure did. But for things like this where it could be my little gopher and allow me more time to do what I do best: front-end. I’m still able to make most of the patches myself based on the output recommendations, but it’s nice to have a gut-check for things where I’m clearly no expert, like security.

According to recent reports, I still use and like Sass very much. I mean, yes, I would like to be straight-up vanilla CSS everywhere, but I can’t tear myself away from partials in particular.

In a recent development, the previous theme had a fairly nice “flat” structure — very few partial directories and most things all in the same top-level source. Totally cool. But an organization nut like me (you should see my house) has to have a place for everything to live. It ain’t perfect, but I’m happy with what I was able to put together without leveling the building in the process.

There are some compromises. Like, /header should really be in /layout. The ordering is really important, though, and some of my ideals were simply not possible. I’m hoping to eventually work in some sort of Cascade Layers structure.

According to recent reports, I’m pleased as punch to see the overall size of CSS drop in the process. It went from 180 KB (31.7 KB) to 169 KB (24.6 KB). Not hugely significant, but not not significant either. I had to do a couple tricky things to cheat my way there, like serving all the form styles I’m about to talk about into a separate forms.css file and serving it just on pages where WooCommerce, Restrict Content Pro, and Gravity Forms are enqueued.

According to recent reports, are you starting to notice a trend? We’re still talking about fairly invisible work. CSS-Tricks has so many nooks and crannies that it’s nearly impossible to make things perfectly consistent across the board. But because of those nooks and crannies, so many fixed values, magic numbers, one-off styles, and older utilities were hiding about. I decided to tackle a good chunk of that while reorganizing the Sass.

For example, there are now semantic design tokens that abstract away one-off colors. So many grays, let me tell you. Now there’s a maintainable palette that’s referenced throughout. Same with fonts, font styles, and font sizes. Same with paddings and margins. It feels a lot better to make a change at the “system” level with confidence that the change is taking effect everywhere it needs to.

But this is also where some clearly visible changes happened! Most notably, link styles are consistent all over the place with a small handful of intended and maintained variations. Not only is it more pleasing visually, but it improves accessibility throughout because the inherited styles default to proper visual cues that do not rely solely on color or opacity changes.

According to recent reports, oh, and my favorite piece of this? Forms and tables have both been redone. That’s tough to do in a WordPress theme where these components don’t always come from one source. For example, forms could come from any one of the Gravity Forms, WooCommerce, or Restrict Content Pro plugins, and they all have their own stylesheets. Resetting those allowed me to bring a certain level of harmony in all those instances.

Recent findings suggest that OK, something even more visual. This is the first time CSS-Tricks has had more than one color scheme! It certainly could have been done a long time ago, but I’d also argue that the design hasn’t really called for a light/dark toggle over the last 8 years or so. It’s a nice blend of both light and dark elements that marry the best of both worlds no matter your theme preference.

But I had to take a stab, right? The site has predominantly been dark despite the content being against a white background, so I treated things as though a “dark” mode already existed. The result is a creamy light theme that is largely just a change in background and component styles. And I used some of what I learned from the recent “toggle” debate to handle system, dark, and light themes with a single toggle.

What hasn’t changed is the main content container you see in things like articles. That was already white, even in a “dark” mode, and I’m not confident that simply toggling it between white and black is the best approach. Something on the radar for sure.

Oh, and it’s all wired up to a view transition that slides the new theme over the previous one.

I hope you think the site’s header and footer are cute. Yes, cute. That’s what I was going for when adding a colorful series of dots as the backdrop.

Sorta like a subtle candy texture, right? Or a colorful group of stars? I dunno, but I’m calling it “Jawbreaker” for lack of a better term and because it reminds me of the jawbreaker candy I loved as a kid. Naming still sucks.

It’s all part of the same SVG. I really, really (really) wanted to random()-ly position dots around, but that would have taken a lot of empty individual elements (e.g., ) in the markup. Not my favorite. So, I generate the elements in PHP:.

I really, really wanted to random()-ize all the things, but inlining random coordinates on each was the way to go. Same deal with the inlined styles that set a fill, and sizing for each circle in the texture, and variables that set a --delay and --dur on the subtle animation that twinkles them in and out.

I’ll have to look at generating the SVG using or whatever later since that pattern repeats in the footer, too.

That’s carried through to the 404 page as well:.

According to recent reports, if your browser supports border-shape and random() (only Chrome, I think), then the homepage gives you a blobby-blob shape behind the grid of author avatars. Hover it and it gets, you know, even blobbier.

It takes an existing pattern I’m calling .gradient-card:.

…and sets a gradient on the component’s :before pseudo:.

That sits underneath the :after pseudo that’s translucent, allowing the :before‘s gradient to show through a smidge:.

The differing border-radius values allow :before to bleed outside, giving the impression of a border around the entire deal. That’s the basic shape. The border-shape is where things get blobby:.

Those variables? They’re mapped to shape()s. I grabbed the first one from Temani Afif’s blob generator:.

Industry observers note that it’s called “static” because that’s the default state. Hover or focus on the component and it swaps out those points out with a “hover” version of the shape:.

Those variables? They’re mapped to random() values:.

So, the hover state is different on each page load. And we animate between the two:.

According to recent reports, I’m pretty stoked on this one. The Almanac has grown, evolved, and just plain gotten great the past few years. But the primary page for it… not so great. It was definitely overshadowed by work on the pages inside it and never revisited beyond clickable cards to get to each feature subset.

According to recent reports, now the page is a real index of the CSS features that gets you where you need to go promptly. Someone somewhere sometime did some sort of CSS periodic table. I forget where I’d seen that but the general idea sat with me and I thought I could pull it off. There’s nothing “tricky” about it but I love what the layout adds to the overall site.

Industry observers note that this is another area that sorely needed love. Our guides have always been a vertical stack of items. The book effect was definitely cool, but I started believing that leaning on it as the main visual hook was holding things back from being more functional. With something like 27 guides, we’re talking about a lot of scrolling with no clear idea of what you’re going to see as you go.

Again, nothing “tricky” but I like the overall usefulness of the new layout. There’s a featured guide, a widget of newly added and updated guides, and a categorized grid of everything below that.

The pages that show all of an author’s published articles got a little spruce-up, too.

It has been revealed that it’s a little change, really. The right sidebar was moved to the left and the author image and bio moved in, allowing the articles to creep up to the top. I hope to do more here since the small layout tweak opens up more opportunities.

Also need to do the larger Authors index, but another time.

Industry observers note that this one’s just for those of us working in the WordPress editor. I don’t need a complete visual editor to get things done, but it is a nice affordance to have some of the front-end styles sneak into the editing UI for a better idea of what you’re working with.

Sources indicate that using Lighthouse to measure things like performance, accessibility, and best practices is woefully fraught with caveats, but there’s no reason to chuck it completely. I find them more fun than fact and I don’t mind the recommendations for improving things.

So, after a few runs and tweaks, here’s how things shook out theme-to-theme.

I’m happy here. There are some things I just don’t have the control to fix when it comes to performance, so seeing v20 come in consistent with v19 is just fine by me. I’m happier with the boosts to accessibility and best practices. SEO? Meh. Don’t really care unless it’s hurting more key things like accessibility.

Again, very happy. There’s little I can do with time to first byte but everything else seems to clock in at least marginally better. The total page weight is a clear win and that’s probably what I care most about here.

It has been revealed that oh gosh, there’s a lot more but they’re mostly minor things that don’t bubble up to the front end. Sort of the same way browser changelogs have some generic line of “bug squashing” or whatever. In this case, it’s things like better post queries and breadcrumbs and function management and naming and… you get it.

Recent findings suggest that there’s definitely so much more to do. And plenty of things I’m sure I missed or broke along the way. That’s just life and those will have to come in another iterative release less worthy of a version bump. You can let me know what I muffed up in the comments.

I hope you at least like where this is going!

CSS Optimization: Is Using Declarations Just Once (UDJO) Still Effective Today?

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that CSS optimization is a deceptive topic.
  • In this article, I’d like to pick a technique that’s at least 18 years old — UDJO, or “using declarations just once.”.
  • According to recent reports, aware of an older source?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that CSS optimization is a deceptive topic. On the one hand, it feels like something simple that we should already have all the tooling for — especially when it comes to minification. On the other hand, the idea that we already exploited “everything” there is around CSS optimization may be considered naive. Such a claim looks hard to defend for a language that evolves almost daily.

In this article, I’d like to pick a technique that’s at least 18 years old — UDJO, or “using declarations just once.”.

According to recent reports, aware of an older source? Please comment!

The technique is inspired by the principle of DRY, “don’t repeat yourself”, in that it works by identifying and reducing (if not eliminating) declaration repetition.

So, if there’s something like display: flex and it appears two or more times, it gets reconciled in one rule:.

The outcome of the technique depends on how intelligently the deduplication is done and how long the selectors are. Intelligence determines if UDJO leads to an actual maintainability advantage — can the change of a declaration really be done to all the selectors attached? And the selector length influences how significant file size savings are.

If you’re interested, my article on “DRY CSS” describes the mechanics in more detail. The question here is: Is UDJO still effective and still relevant today?

When we try to answer this question, however, we end up with a problem: When sites are complex and their style sheet declarations have not been de-duplicated before, UDJO can require a lot of work.

To save some time, I built tooling for this work. While it didn’t seem like it would immediately be as comprehensive as manually going through and testing style sheets, it seemed realistic enough that a tool could catch some repetition.

In a recent development, skipping ahead, I created CSS Dedup not only to identify repetition, but also to deduplicate what could safely be optimized (CSS Dedup has some documentation on this but in essence, deduplication affects selector locations, which is part of how the cascade works). This, then, gives us some data:.

Sources indicate that for the first batch, I arbitrarily picked 20 websites to analyze. I then used CSS Dedup to check what the file size changes would be if we deduplicated what seemed provably safe, and also what seemed probably safe, but only if it led to file size savings.

I picked those two options to provide the “natural” result of deduplication, but also the one site owners may be most interested in to reduce repetition but also decrease transfer size. After all, UDJO as a CSS optimization technique can improve both maintainability and performance.

Key note: These values cannot be used to tell CSS quality—they depend on selector length and also on verifying if deduplication, in the respective case, actually leads to better maintainability. Also note that this leaves out changes after compression—this was not part of the experiment but would be fair to test, too.

For the question whether UDJO still works today, this should be a yes. It works as well as to even come with file size savings.

According to recent reports, maybe you’re curious, too, about what the situation looks like in our field, among web developers. Let’s take some samples on this, too.

It would be valuable to expand this analysis to take more samples and investigate the differences across samples, but there may be something to web professionals using shorter selectors so as to be able to benefit more from UDJO.

As mentioned at the beginning, UDJO’s effectiveness generally depends on the kind of repetition as well as on the length of selectors.

This can be managed, however: While tools like CSS Dedup make no difference between declaration use cases (and are therefore blunt), it is possible to configure them so as to reap the performance benefits.

It has been revealed that as the data taken for this article suggest, file size savings may be achieved in most cases. Considering that this is based on safe changes, this means a low-cost performance optimization vector — especially when applied to minified output. It’s still a good idea to couch that against the use of further compression (e.g. gzip/Brotli), but at face value, deduplication indicates how it can reduce the size of CSS.

For anyone generally interested in CSS optimization, maintainability, and performance, UDJO should probably be part of the overall approach to CSS. But since the technique has been niche and since tooling is new, I invite you to review, test, and explore this vector. It seems hard to argue that we have reached the ceiling of how far we can take CSS optimization.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Michigan's online casinos generated $305.3 million in adjusted gross receipts in October, up 16.7% from a year earlier.
  • Michigan’s online casino market kept growing at a double-digit rate in October.
  • The October result followed a soft patch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michigan's online casinos generated $305.3 million in adjusted gross receipts in October, up 16.7% from a year earlier. The double-digit gain comes as national iGaming growth cools, though Michigan's own pace has slowed from a year ago.

Michigan’s online casino market kept growing at a double-digit rate in October. Gross receipts came to $318.1 million, according to figures the Michigan Gaming Control Board released Nov. 18. It was the state’s second-best iGaming month of 2026. Only March, with a record $309.1 million in AGR, was higher. March also holds the monthly gross receipts record of $322.1 million, which topped the $315.8 million from December 2025.

The October result followed a soft patch. September AGR was $288.15 million, 0.9% lower than in August.

Sources indicate that the year-over-year gain stands out against the national backdrop. Citizens JMP Securities estimated that US iGaming revenue grew 12% in the third quarter of 2026, the slowest pace it has recorded. Growth had been 19% in the first quarter and 16% in the second. The same data put Michigan’s third-quarter iGaming growth at 17%. Only Delaware, at 36%, and West Virginia, at 26%, grew faster.

Michigan’s own pace has still slowed sharply. In October 2025, online casino AGR grew 31.8% year over year, nearly double this October’s rate. That month produced $261.7 million in AGR and $278.5 million in gross receipts, a record at the time.

The Michigan figures also invite comparison with Pennsylvania. Its online casinos generated $278,845,570 in October revenue, a state record for Pennsylvania. That figure came in a release issued Nov. 17, a day before Michigan published its October numbers.

The year-over-year numbers show where Michigan’s growth comes from. Online sports betting AGR fell 3.3% from October 2025. For all of 2025, sportsbooks produced $435.9 million in AGR, while iGaming generated $3.1 billion in gross receipts. Online casino play therefore accounts for most of the state’s online gambling revenue.

October sportsbook figures swung sharply from one month to the next. Sports betting AGR jumped 91.3% from September. Handle rose 11.1% to $605.4 million, and sportsbook gross receipts reached $70.7 million. Combined online casino and sports betting gross receipts totaled $388.8 million.

Industry observers note that the broader online market had been growing faster earlier in the year. From January through July, combined online casino and sports betting AGR totaled $2.21 billion, up 20.9% from the same period in 2025. October’s casino growth is consistent with a market that is still expanding, but at a slower rate than a year ago.

Tribal online operators also made $8.9 million in payments to their governing bodies for October.

#115603. Industry News: Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1643 w)
📖 Baca

Industry News: Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when I started designing websites thirty years ago, David Siegel had just published Creating Killer Web Sites, the book that popularised HTML tables and spacer GIFs for laying out web pages.
  • When CSS frameworks began providing ready-made grid systems, things got a little easier.
  • In a recent development, twelve-column grids weren’t invented in the 2000s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when I started designing websites thirty years ago, David Siegel had just published Creating Killer Web Sites, the book that popularised HTML tables and spacer GIFs for laying out web pages. CSS eventually gave us more control over layouts through floats and positioning. Neither was intended for page layout, and inconsistent browser behaviour could make using them frustrating. Still, that didn’t stop me and a generation of other designers from using floats and positioning.

When CSS frameworks began providing ready-made grid systems, things got a little easier. Blueprint CSS) offered a 24-column grid, while Nathan Smith’s 960 Grid System offered 12- and 16-column options. These frameworks gave designers and developers a shared structure, making layout planning and implementation considerably easier.

In a recent development, twelve-column grids weren’t invented in the 2000s. Graphic designers had used column-based and modular grids for decades, and twelve is a convenient number because you don’t need to be a maths genius to divide it into halves, thirds, and quarters to create the 2-up, 3-up, and 4-up components we see everywhere online.

Frameworks like Bootstrap and Foundation followed, helping establish twelve-column grids as the de facto standard for page layouts. I get why that happened. But somewhere along the way, one layout option became the default starting point for almost everything.

CSS Grid changed what’s possible for page layouts, but I still see designers start by dividing a page into twelve equal columns, then deciding how to fit their content into them. The designs they end up with might be perfectly fine, but they can also look remarkably similar.

Still, I don’t think twelve-column grids themselves are the problem. It’s reaching for a familiar solution before considering what makes the manufacturer I’m designing for distinctive and what its website needs to communicate. So what happens when I start with those questions instead?

In a recent development, before I decide how many columns a layout needs, I want to understand the manufacturer I’m designing for. What makes it different from its competitors? What does it want people to remember? Does it have a personality that could influence how its website looks and feels?

In a recent development, these questions matter because a layout does more than arrange content. The size, position, and relationships between elements influence how people experience a website. A restrained, orderly composition can communicate something very different from one that’s full of energy and movement. So to demonstrate what I mean, I’ll use Wheelman. It’s a fictional tech giant I invented for my book, Standout Designs for the Web.

Pre-orders for Standout Designs for the Web are now open in the CSS-Tricks store.

Wheelman provides products and services for getaway drivers, including legal advice, robbery insurance, and an online shop selling break-in essentials. It also publishes a magazine with advice, news, and stories about life behind the wheel.

Wheelman isn’t an ordinary manufacturer, so why should its website look like an everyday collection of components? It takes its business seriously, but isn’t afraid to have fun with its design. It’s rebellious, but doesn’t want to look off-putting. Its audience is criminals, but they demand professionalism. Wheelman has plenty of personality to work with, and I want its designs to reflect that.

That doesn’t mean making Wheelman different for difference’s sake. Its customers still need to find what they’re looking for, understand what it provides, and buy its products and services. But I can make those experiences more memorable by choosing layouts that fit the company, rather than settling for familiar arrangements.

It has been revealed that let’s imagine I’m designing a new landing page for Wheelman’s online shop. It includes two products, one with a gigantic headline, product images, and the type of functionality and information you’ll find on most stores.

Industry observers note that before I decide how to arrange these elements, I want to look beyond them and consider how they relate. I ask myself questions like:.

Only then do I start thinking about visual design questions: “Would a large photograph set the scene? Should I make the introduction more prominent? Can whitespace lead the eye and create spaces to pause? How can I bring images and text together into a considered composition?”.

These questions help me understand what the layout needs to accomplish before I decide which grid might help me achieve it.

Industry observers note that I could arrange everything in a single column for a straightforward reading experience. That would make responsive design considerably easier. But I won’t.

Wheelman has a rebellious personality, and I want its shop to reflect that. A more energetic layout seems appropriate, but I still need to establish a clear hierarchy between the products and their information. Two equal-width columns give both products equal prominence.

Changing their proportions creates a hierarchy, even when most elements stay the same size.

I could base those proportions on a twelve-column grid, but I won’t. Columns only divide space vertically, and I want a layout that adds another dimension.

Dividing a layout into columns is a useful starting point, but adding rows creates another dimension and opens up more creative possibilities. Where columns and rows intersect, they form rectangular or square units called modules.

Combining these modules creates larger spatial zones that can establish hierarchy, control whitespace, and add variety to a composition.

Recent findings suggest that using a modular grid, I can add drama, establish hierarchy by varying scale, and make the composition feel far less predictable. Starting with four columns and four rows gives me sixteen modules to work with, but I don’t need to fill them all.

I can create drama by spreading the large graphic headline and product image across four modules, while the product information and shopping tools occupy one module each.

The modular structure becomes even more apparent in the grid of alternative products. Most occupy just one module, while others fill two, either horizontally or vertically. Varying their sizes gives some products more prominence and makes the overall arrangement feel less predictable.

Sources indicate that the result still feels like a product page, with a clear reading order and space for the content to breathe. But it also feels unmistakably like something Wheelman would publish.

I don’t expect this composition to work at every screen size, so I can adjust the size and quantity of modules to improve the reading experience.

And if one grid offers this much flexibility, imagine what combining two or more grids can do.

Industry observers note that one thing I want from Wheelman’s website is variety. Its magazine, shop, and services serve different purposes, and I don’t want every page to feel like I’ve poured its content into the same template.

Wheelman needs layouts which feel organised without being predictable. Compound grids give me the structure I need while leaving room for less conventional arrangements.

A compound grid combines two or more grids of any type — column, modular, or hierarchical — on the same page. These grids can overlap, sit side by side, or be stacked one on top of the other. Combining grids creates possibilities which neither grid offers on its own.

I can start by overlaying a two-column grid with one containing three columns. Their combined grid lines create four columns of two different widths, giving me more flexibility without losing the underlying structure.

Those proportions offer more possibilities for arranging content. I might use a wider area for a photograph or headline, then place a pullquote into one of the narrower spaces. Another page could use the same underlying grid but combine its spaces differently to suit another story.

Combining grids with different column counts gets even more interesting as those numbers increase. In Standout Designs for the Web, I explore several combinations, including mixing four- and five-column grids to create different compositions for Wheelman’s pages while maintaining a connected visual structure.

According to recent reports, the point isn’t to make every page look different for its own sake. It’s to give each section a layout that suits its content while keeping them all feeling like part of the same firm.

Twelve-column grids are useful, and I’m certainly not suggesting you should stop using them entirely. But they’re only one option among many, and starting every design with the same structure limits your possibilities before you’ve even considered the story your design is telling.

There’s also nothing inherently wrong with the 2-up, 3-up, and 4-up patterns a twelve-column grid inspires. They can sometimes be exactly what’s needed. But reaching for them automatically can leave little room for the character and personality that make websites memorable.

Recent findings suggest that wheelman gives me plenty of reasons to choose different layouts. Its stories, products, and services don’t all need the same arrangements, and its personality gives me opportunities to make those arrangements more distinctive. The grids are simply tools that help me put those ideas into practice.

And this applies to much more than layout. The same thinking should influence the colours I choose, the typography I use, the images I commission, and the way I bring those elements together.

That’s why I wrote Standout Designs for the Web. I want to encourage designers to look beyond familiar solutions and make more deliberate decisions about colour, typography, imagery, and layout. Not to be different for difference’s sake, but to create websites that look and feel like they belong to the companies behind them. And no one else.

The book will be published on November 20, priced at $14.99 for the DRM-free EPUB and PDF editions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that utah has sued the companies behind the Stake sweepstakes site, alleging it ran an illegal casino for Utahns since 2022. The case follows Florida's own suit against Stake and adds to the legal pressure on the dual-currency sweepstakes model.

Sources indicate that the timing of Utah’s suit against Stake stands out. Stake added Utah to its list of restricted states on Nov. 13, four days before the suit was filed, yet state consumer protection investigators could still use the site as recently as Nov. 16, when a banner noted access would end on Dec. 7, the 43-page complaint says.

Sources indicate that utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division of Consumer Protection brought the case. It names two defendants: Sweepsteaks Limited, based in Cyprus, and its Australian parent, Easygo Group Holdings Pty Ltd. The state refers to them jointly as Stake.

In a recent development, the central allegation is that Stake has offered Utahns a round-the-clock casino since 2022. Utah has prohibited gambling since it became a state, and its Constitution bans gambling.

Recent findings suggest that the complaint takes aim at how the site works. Players spend real money on two virtual currencies.

Utah wants the court to declare the site illegal gambling under state law. It also asks the court to bar Stake from offering its games in Utah and to order the firm to return money taken from residents. The state is also seeking fines under the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act and a remedy for harm to the public. The complaint adds claims for unjust enrichment, public nuisance and declaratory judgment.

A demand that players’ losses be repaid raises the stakes for the wider industry. Taken together, the relief Utah seeks increases the legal risk for sweepstakes operators, suppliers and affiliates nationwide.

Sources indicate that utah is not the only state to bring Stake itself into court. Florida’s suit is broader in scope. It names Sweepsteaks Ltd and Easygo alongside Medium Rare and Kick Streaming, NEXT.io reported. It also names co-founders Bijan Tehrani and Ed Craven, plus payment firms Praxis and Breeze Labs Payments. Utah’s complaint is limited to the two corporate defendants.

According to recent reports, other states have targeted the same business model through a different operator. Kentucky and Arkansas have both sued VGW, which runs its own dual-currency sweepstakes sites.

In a recent development, the Stake case is separate from Utah’s clash with federal regulators over prediction markets. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has sued Utah to stop the state from using its own laws to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets. The Stake suit also came less than three weeks after Utah filed criminal charges against Kalshi’s founders. Those charges include felony counts of online gambling promotion.

Court records did not list a lawyer for either defendant, and the manufacturer did not answer a request for comment on the suit.

October’s figures show the higher rate did not coincide with any immediate drop in revenue. That matters for other states weighing online casino tax rates. It also matters for the two operators, which now share a larger tax bill in a market they split almost evenly.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The other day on the CSS-Tricks Slack channel, Danny Schwartz shared an interesting recent Master.dev article by Ashutosh Biswas on how to stagger CSS scrolling animations using a clever combo of several emergent CSS features and a lot of math, which Ashutosh admits is “a huge formula and can look intimidating.”.

I’ll agree with Ashutosh there.

Recent findings suggest that when Danny Slacked the link for the Frontend Masters article, he described it as “CSS on drugs.” Speaking of drugs, I am on heavy prescription painkillers while recovering from a serious injury, so that might not help my current comprehension skills. Nevertheless, after reading Ashutosh’s article a few times, here’s a meme showing how I’d feel using such an elaborate algorithm for something as mundane as staggering the animations of some characters as they scroll into view.

According to recent reports, don’t get me wrong. I know the complexity is because Ashutosh is going for a generic solution in which we can connect a “progress value to an animation, scroll progress, or any other input to drive the staggering.”.

In fact, I can dream up a scenario in which this might be what we want: Imagine a CSS karaoke machine that displays a ball bouncing on text that incrementally highlights, based on the user’s progress through the vocals measured via speech recognition. Running that kind of animation “not as a collection of independently timed objects, but as a single predictable, holistic effect driven by one progress value” might be exactly what the doctor ordered. This would be true because the staggered animations could be interrelated, and the overall animation would be driven by a custom input that’s not built into the browser.

But unlike this hypothetical scenario, replacing the passage of time with scroll progress to control animations is already built into modern CSS. I contend that we’d need a better reason to roll our own implementation than the examples Ashutosh gives.

Ashutosh showcases a scroll-driven use case as “one of those ideal scenarios where the stagger formula shines.” But a red flag that we’re in danger of reinventing something we can get for free is that the spec for scroll-driven animations is cognizant that if we opt to base an animation on scroll progress rather than on time, then, as Ashutosh says, “the animation we are going to achieve is different from traditional ones because we don’t include time in our considerations.” This is no surprise to the creators of scroll timeline, and the MDN docs make Ashutosh’s point in different words when introducing scroll timeline.

Sources indicate that the docs also point out that animation-delay is only meaningful when we are using the default time-based document timeline. Therefore, animation-delay does not affect scroll-driven animations. But this is why CSS introduced animation-range-start, which allows us to delay a scroll-driven animation relative to scroll progress and not time.

So, as esoteric and trippy as the math-heavy approach appears, that could be because we are doing something that should be simple in an unusual way.

Let’s see if I’m right by rewriting Ashutosh’s demo to remove reliance on custom CSS functions and use animation-range-start instead.

Ashutosh’s rework of Frontend Masters’ animated tally of donations in the site footer is a nifty, subtle use of scrollytelling that makes the user feel invested in revealing that number.

Sidenote: The only qualm I have about this use of scroll-driven animations for the donation tally is that it might be too subtle — if the user scrolls too swiftly, the animated entrance of each digit might occur too quickly to notice. Therefore, the donation tally could be a good case study for comparing the merits of scroll-driven versus scroll-triggered animations as design options. However, that story will have to wait for another day, as the focus of this article is only to show that the staggered scrolling CSS animations can be greatly simplified.

In the video below, my eight-year-old narrates, as a reminder that simplicity is key to the web we’re choosing to leave to the next generation. He compares the complex math in the original demo source code with my animation-range-start fork. He indicates the two versions working side by side, demonstrating that sometimes the only thing we lose by judiciously deleting complex code is a headache.

It has been revealed that and for those using a Chromium-based browser, my fork of the Pen is below. You can peruse the CSS to see how it does away with the grand unified theory of staggered scrolling animations, and instead deals only with the problem at hand. Since I preserved the original functionality, you’ll need to scroll gradually to appreciate the staggered animations.

I once tackled a related problem with a mathematical formula in a previous article, which touched on how we can use sibling-index() to “increment animation-range-start to stagger the delay before characters fade in as the user scrolls.”.

The truth is, if we refuse to fall into the coding trap of possibly abstracting the wrong thing, we can use one line of CSS to replace a formula that took 1.3k words in the Frontend Masters article for me to still not fully grasp:.

The 2.5% increment for each sibling is because there are eight characters to stagger, and I wanted to choreograph the animations such that they are delayed in evenly-spaced increments till the last character makes its animated entrance when it reaches 30% of the containment range (10% + 20%).

According to recent reports, it was inadvertently apt to describe the original post as “CSS on drugs.” Once you reinvent one built-in CSS feature, you can’t stop there. You find yourself having to recreate more stuff that CSS should be able to do by itself. Sure enough, even after we get through the custom formulas that make scroll timelines do what they already do, Ashutosh reveals, “Unfortunately, we can’t use easing keywords or cubic-bezier() or linear() functions here. We are left on our own to create easing functions.”.

We shouldn’t have to because, despite the word “timing” in the name of the animation-timing-function property, MDN is clear that “animation-timing-function has the same effect when creating CSS scroll-driven animations as it does for regular time-based animations.” I know from experience that scroll-driven animations work with animation-timing-function because I used scroll-driven animations with steps() to animate a sprite climbing a ladder in my CSS scrollytelling game.

The problem in the land of CSS on drugs is that after merging all the staggered animations into one, the easing applies to the entire master timeline rather than to each element. It’s not a flaw in CSS, but a logical consequence of the “holistic effect driven by one progress value.” Be careful what you wish for.

To be fair, over the years I have seen impressive results from developers reinventing things the browsers already do, usually because the reinvention gives us control we couldn’t obtain otherwise.

I mention this to show that reinventing something like scroll timelines isn’t an inherently bad idea if we know why we’re doing it. After all, scroll timelines are only a reinvention of what developers were doing for decades prior in JavaScript. Having said that, I believe my rewrite of the staggered scroll-driven tally demo demonstrates that the original approach was overkill for that example. Do let me know in the comments if you see any advantage to the custom CSS functions version over using animation-range-start.

And yet the thought that stuck with me about the Frontend Masters post is that it opens the door to linking the progress of a CSS animation to any arbitrary input value that could be used in a conceptually similar way to scroll timelines.

It has been revealed that this really appeals to me, because even when I first started writing about scroll timelines in 2024, I mentioned that “I would love to see other input controls that can manipulate animation timelines. Imagine text fields progressing animations as you fill them out.” Or how about an animation driven by how closely the newly introduced password you are typing matches a password scheme?

Sidenote: Adam Argyle’s Prop For That library, which Geoff recently wrote up, makes it more convenient than ever to expose validation information about a field via CSS custom properties.

I can add my hypothetical karaoke machine scenario to the wishlist of custom progress inputs for controlling animations. How about an animation driven by the user’s progress through a quiz or a shopping cart?

Custom animation timelines would open the door to all sorts of engaging user experiences—but the code Ashutosh has shared may be the closest we are likely to get to driving CSS animations using values other than time or scroll progress.

Let me know in the comments if you can think of other types of progress inputs that could drive CSS animations to create immersive, interactive experiences.

#115598. When Everything Has Changed, What Do We Do Next?

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1883 w)
