No. A container is an isolated process that shares the host kernel. Docker Sandboxes are microVMs with their own kernel, filesystem, network, and Docker Engine. A sandbox can run containers, which is why the two are easy to confuse.

According to recent reports, yes. Each sandbox has a private Docker Engine, so the agent can build images, run Testcontainers, and start Compose applications without the host socket or Docker-in-Docker.

In a recent development, no. Containers remain the right tool for packaged applications, CI jobs, and short-lived execution. Sandboxes add a stronger boundary for autonomous agents, and containers keep running inside them.

A container isolates a workload. Containment involves the whole environment around an agent: the boundary it runs in, what it can reach, which tools it uses, and how you reproduce it. A container can be part of containment, and Docker Sandboxes add the microVM boundary an autonomous agent needs.

Docker describes four requirements: containment (a boundary the model can’t rewrite), control (visibility into what the agent is doing and the ability to stop it), choice (swapping models, agents, and tools without rebuilding), and capacity (a setup other developers can reproduce and scale past one machine).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A coding agent in Docker Sandboxes runs inside an isolated VM, the sandbox controls which hosts it can reach, and credentials stay on the host behind a proxy.
  • The Firecrawl kit gives the agent web search, page scraping, and site crawling through one added host, api.firecrawl.dev, and every page comes back as clean markdown.
  • The Firecrawl kit is a mixin (kind: mixin): it extends whichever workload you already run rather than defining a newly introduced sandbox.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A coding agent in Docker Sandboxes runs inside an isolated VM, the sandbox controls which hosts it can reach, and credentials stay on the host behind a proxy. The same controls keep the agent from opening a docs page, reading a changelog, or looking up an API that shipped after its training cutoff, so it writes code against the version it remembers. The usual fix is to widen the allowlist until the agent can fetch anything, which hands back most of what the sandbox took away.

The Firecrawl kit gives the agent web search, page scraping, and site crawling through one added host, api.firecrawl.dev, and every page comes back as clean markdown.

The Firecrawl kit is a mixin (kind: mixin): it extends whichever workload you already run rather than defining a newly introduced sandbox. Its descriptor, firecrawl/firecrawl.yaml, declares four typed capabilities:.

According to recent reports, the kit adds to the sandbox’s allowlist and does not narrow it, so everything else is set by your global sbx policy. Docker’s balanced preset allows package registries, GitHub, and a curated list of vendor domains, and returns a 403 for general websites, including most documentation sites, so Firecrawl is the agent’s route to those. Under deny-all, it is the agent’s only web host.

Kits are experimental and in Early Access, so the kit format and sbx commands may change. The steps below are current for October 2026; the repository README carries the latest.

Kit: docker.io/firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl:1.0.0 on Docker Hub, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. Source: github.com/firecrawl/firecrawl-docker-sandbox.

Industry observers note that 1. Store the key once on the host. The command prompts for the key. Service secrets are global by default, so every sandbox that requests the firecrawl service can use it once you approve. The kit never sees the value; the proxy injects it at request time.

2. Start a sandbox with the kit. The kit is an ordinary OCI image with its descriptor in the manifest, so a version tag is all you need. Each --kit adds a mixin to the workload, and the trailing . mounts your project directory.

Recent findings suggest that on the first run, sbx asks you to approve sending the firecrawl credential to api.firecrawl.dev. Accept the defaults. The credential is required: with no secret stored, sbx refuses to create the sandbox instead of letting the agent hit a 401 mid-task. A detached or CI run cannot answer the approval prompt, so approve interactively once or write the binding to ~/.config/sbx/credentials.yaml first.

3. Give the agent a task that needs the live web. Documentation sites are blocked under balanced, so this one has to go through Firecrawl.

It has been revealed that the kit’s instructions tell the agent to scrape blocked hosts through Firecrawl, so it calls fc.scrape(...) unprompted. Its response, trimmed:.

Industry observers note that 4. Verify each layer. In the same session, ! runs shell commands inside the sandbox.

Expected: FIRECRAWL_API_KEY=proxy-managed. A real fc-... value here means the key came from somewhere other than the kit.

Industry observers note that expected: the page as markdown, starting with # Changelog and the latest version heading. The same URL returns a 403 to curl from inside the sandbox, so output here proves the SDK, the credential, and the network rule at once.

The kit also describes itself inside the sandbox. This prints the published descriptor, and the agent instructions sit next to it as firecrawl-context.md:.

In a recent development, running from source. To review or modify the kit before you run it, clone the repository and point --kit at the firecrawl/ directory; sbx builds source kits on demand:.

Sources indicate that with the kit installed, the agent can look things up on the web while it works. The sandbox only needs to talk to one upcoming address, api.firecrawl.dev, and Firecrawl fetches the pages for it. This matters because the default balanced policy blocks most documentation sites. Without the kit, you’d have to allow each site one by one, and every new site you allow makes the sandbox a little less locked down.

It has been revealed that without the kit, you had a choice to make. The default balanced policy blocks most documentation sites, so you could either leave the agent working from what it remembered, or allow sites one by one and loosen the sandbox a little each time. The kit avoids that choice. Your Firecrawl API key stays on your machine, behind the proxy, and the agent still reads the web as it is today.

The result is fewer made-up APIs, fewer failed upgrades, and less time spent correcting an agent that was confidently out of date.

The kit is published under the firecrawl organization on Docker Hub as firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl, with source, changelog, and CI on GitHub under Apache-2.0. The SDK pin is verified against PyPI’s package hashes at install time, and every release passes Docker’s kit-tck conformance suite in CI. Review the descriptor and allowlist before running it, as with any kit.

Pull the kit from Docker Hub: hub.docker.com/r/firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl. Problems and feature requests go to the GitHub repository.

There's no telling what caused the Nvidia board to vote unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO less than a week after saying his return wasn’t under consideration – except reportedly the threat of having one's head ripped off and brain peed on – but that really doesn't matter, at least as far as shareholders need to be concerned: Jensen's back in charge and all’s right in the world of chip stocks.

"I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang noted of the decision to reinstate him, calling it an honor.

Nvidia kicked its former-cum-current CEO and president to the curb on November 12, but not over allegations that he may have been sleeping with a suspected Chinese spy – it was affairs at Nvidia with his subordinates that appears to have been the last straw with Nvidia directors.

In a recent development, nvidia stock has tumbled since Huang’s ouster, and much of the rest of the tech stock world followed suit. Nvidia insiders and tech heavyweights have been pushing for Huang’s return for about as long as he was unemployed, but calls for his return from the US federal government may have been the catalyst for a change of heart among Nvidia leadership who didn’t want Huang back.

"In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk," Nvidia said in its statement announcing Huang’s return.

Recent findings suggest that "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," board chair Harvey Jones added. Jones was made Nvidia's first board chair upon Huang’s resignation, and will remain in that role.

Recent findings suggest that the White House has since confirmed that the senior-level official involved in Huang’s reinstatement was President Trump.According to a White House statement to Semafor, Trump personally dialed in to an Nvidia board meeting hours before Huang was reinstated to argue for his return.“President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board,” White House comms director Steven Cheung told Semafor. “We have to protect our geniuses.”.

Recent findings suggest that "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security," Trump stated in a post on Truth Social. "The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.".

Sources indicate that the surprise return echoes Sam Altman's return as CEO of OpenAI after the board fired him for a brief five days in 2023 over allegations of dishonesty. Both reinstatements happened around the US Thanksgiving holiday, suggesting that the spirit of forgiveness waxes with the anticipation of that roasted turkey smell wafting through the house. ®.

The Trust Layer: Securing Agentic AI with Docker AI Governance

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt.
  • A model decision is not automatically an authorized action.
  • The answer can’t rely only on the model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt. It can execute code, access files, connect to services, and call external tools. That creates a newly introduced security question for enterprises: how do you give an agent enough freedom to be useful without giving it more access than it actually needs?

A model decision is not automatically an authorized action. That distinction becomes key the moment an agent can turn a model output into an action in a real system.

The answer can’t rely only on the model. Agent behavior can vary, while security controls need to be clear and enforceable. That means putting controls around the environment where the agent runs, what it can access, which tools it can use, and what happens when a policy allows or blocks an action. For a CISO, this creates a trust gap. Approving the use of AI agents means being able to answer more than whether the model is capable: what access does the agent have, where are those boundaries enforced, and what evidence is available afterward? The goal is to let teams adopt agents without making model behavior itself the security boundary.

Docker AI Governance approaches this through three areas: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility.

Together, they address three practical questions security teams need answered: Where can the agent operate? What can it do? And can we see what happened?

In this article, I use “trust layer” as shorthand for the infrastructure between what an agent wants to do and what the organization actually allows it to do.

According to recent reports, there is a related trust question too: what software artifacts are these agentic workflows building and using? Docker Hardened Images address that software supply-chain side of the problem, alongside the runtime controls discussed below.

Figure 1: The three layers of Docker AI Governance: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility.

According to recent reports, an agent needs enough access to get real work done. A coding agent may need to install packages, build containers, edit project files, or connect to external services. The security challenge is deciding where those actions are allowed before the agent starts taking them.

Industry observers note that docker Sandboxes give each agent an isolated microVM environment a lightweight virtual machine with its own Docker Engine, filesystem, and network. Docker AI Governance adds policy around that environment so security teams can control network and filesystem access centrally.

Industry observers note that network policies can allow or block specific domains, IP ranges, and ports. Filesystem policies control which host paths can be mounted into a sandbox and whether that access is read-only or read-write. These controls are enforced at the network proxy and filesystem mount layers rather than depending on the agent to follow an instruction.

Recent findings suggest that for an organization, that means the same boundaries can follow developers across their sandboxes instead of being configured differently on every machine. Teams still get the access they need for their work, but an individual agent cannot simply expand those boundaries on its own.

A developer can check the effective boundary before starting the agent:.

The important part is that the result comes from the active policy, not from an instruction the agent is expected to follow.

This answers the first governance question: Where can the agent operate?

Once an agent has a controlled place to run, the next question is what it should be allowed to do through external tools.

It has been revealed that MCP (Model Context Protocol) gives agents a common way to connect to external tools, services, and capabilities, but that also expands what an agent can act on. For enterprise use, making a tool available should not automatically mean every agent can use it.

Docker AI Governance puts policy around MCP activity handled through Docker’s MCP Gateway. Administrators can control which MCP servers may be registered and what agents can do through them, including tool calls, resources, prompts, and approval requirements. These organization policies are written in Cedar, a policy language used to express authorization rules. When MCP policy enforcement is active, governed requests are denied unless a matching policy permits them. For example, a policy can permit read-only tool calls for a specific registered MCP server:.

According to recent reports, here, readOnly comes from the MCP tool’s annotations. Those annotations are supplied by the server and are advisory, so this example relies on metadata provided by that server.

Recent findings suggest that this makes tool access an explicit policy decision rather than something left to each agent or developer to configure independently. A team can be given access to the tools it needs, while other servers or actions remain unavailable. Policies can also require confirmation for specific tool calls when an action needs an additional checkpoint.

Sources indicate that one boundary is worth making clear: MCP policies apply to activity handled by Docker’s MCP Gateway. If an agent connects directly to a remote MCP server from inside a sandbox, that connection falls under the sandbox’s network policy instead.

With the environment constrained and tool access governed, we can answer the second question: What can the agent do?

Setting a policy is only part of the job. Security teams also need to know when that policy was applied, what action triggered it, and whether the action was allowed or denied.

Docker AI Governance records sandbox policy decisions and sandbox session events as structured audit records. Each record captures details such as the principal, action, target, decision, and time. The records contain governance metadata rather than the contents of prompts or agent responses.

Audit records can be kept locally or delivered to the cloud. With cloud delivery enabled, teams can search the organization-wide record, export it for further analysis, or forward events into existing SIEM (security information and event management) workflows.

In a recent development, denied actions are especially useful. A team can see not only that an action failed, but that a governance rule blocked it and why. Allowed decisions matter too: they provide a record of how policy was applied while the agent was working.

According to recent reports, current audit coverage includes Docker Sandboxes policy decisions and sandbox session events. The same schema can support additional Docker AI sources as they become available.

That closes the third part of the governance loop: Can we see what happened?

Industry observers note that AI Governance controls access around the agent at runtime. There is a separate question that matters to the workflows those agents participate in: what container images and software artifacts are they building, testing, or deploying?

Docker Hardened Images provide minimal, secure, and production-ready container images, Helm charts, and system packages maintained by Docker.

According to recent reports, in practical terms, this gives teams evidence about what is inside an image and how that image was produced. Docker Hardened Images include signed SBOMs, VEX information, cryptographic signatures, and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance. Instead of simply trusting where an image came from, teams can inspect what is inside it and verify information about how it was built.

For organizations with additional compliance requirements, Docker also provides FIPS-enabled and STIG-ready variants through relevant DHI offerings. These capabilities sit alongside the broader DHI security and supply-chain controls rather than making any single standard the foundation by itself.

Sources indicate that AI Governance and Docker Hardened Images solve different parts of the trust problem. Governance controls the authority an agent has while it works; DHI helps establish trust in the container artifacts that the workflow depends on.

Figure 2: Docker Hardened Images combine minimal container images with signed supply-chain metadata and verifiable build provenance.

Consider a developer using a coding agent to investigate an problem, update a service, and use an approved internal tool along the way.

The agent begins inside a Docker Sandbox. It can work with the project and run the commands needed for the task, but its access is still bounded by policy. If it tries to reach a network destination or mount a host path that the organization has not allowed, the applicable sandbox policy can block that access.

Industry observers note that now suppose the agent needs an MCP tool to look up information from another service. The request goes through Docker’s MCP Gateway, where organization policy determines whether that server and tool are permitted. A routine lookup might be allowed, while a more sensitive tool call could require confirmation or remain unavailable altogether.

For governance activity currently covered by AI Governance Audit Logs, Docker records the policy decision and relevant session metadata. Security teams can see who initiated the activity, what policy-controlled action was evaluated, and whether it was allowed or denied. Those records can then feed the organization’s existing monitoring and SIEM workflow.

If that same agent builds or tests a containerized application, the software entering the workflow matters too. Docker Hardened Images provide a more verifiable software foundation for that workflow, while AI Governance controls what the agent is authorized to do at runtime.

Industry observers note that the model is still making decisions about how to complete the task. What changes is the authority around those decisions. The agent can work autonomously inside the boundaries the organization has defined, while access outside those boundaries remains a policy decision.

That is the practical value of the three layers working together:.

Sandbox Policies define where the agent can operate.

MCP Tool Governance defines what tools it can use.

Audit + Visibility shows how governed activity was handled.

Taken together, the pattern is straightforward: define the boundary, check it before the agent starts working, enforce it while the agent is running, and use the resulting audit trail to understand what happened. If a boundary needs to change, the policy changes, not the expectation that the model will simply behave differently.

Recent findings suggest that the challenge with agentic AI is not simply that agents can make decisions. It is that those decisions can now lead directly to actions.

That makes the boundary around the agent just as notable as the model itself. Docker AI Governance addresses that boundary through Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility: controlling where agents can operate, what tools they can use, and how governed activity is recorded.

Docker Hardened Images address a related supply-chain concern by helping teams work with smaller, verifiable container artifacts.

The goal is not to remove autonomy from agents. It is to make sure autonomy does not automatically come with unlimited authority.

As agents take on more real work, that distinction will matter more and more.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself.
  • It has been revealed that but it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Docker is officially launching its new brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change.

Let’s start with the big picture. We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself. AI is creating possibilities that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago.

It has been revealed that but it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control? Or, put more simply: how do we get to a point where we can actually trust agents?

That one seemingly simple yet infinitely complex question is why we’re here today, introducing you to a latest Docker.

A newly introduced Docker, but a familiar story.

Recent findings suggest that ok, not exactly here, but once upon a time, a decade or so ago, the tech industry was at a similar inflection point. Digital transformation was the term du jour, promising a new way of engaging customers and powering the global economy. There was one major constraint, though: teams needed a better way to build, ship, and run software consistently across any environment.

Enter a organization you might have heard of: Docker.

In a recent development, together with all of you, Docker built the standard trusted by millions of developers. For over a decade, developers have relied on us to make software portable, open, reproducible, and secure. Docker turned the frustration of “Well, it works on my machine!” into the assurance that “Yes, it works everywhere.”.

Today, of course, the challenge confronting us is upcoming and evolving, and we all need to evolve with it. We cannot simply continue to do what we’ve always done and expect to succeed in this new era. That applies to business leaders, developers, tech companies, everyone. It certainly applies to Docker. That’s what this rebrand is about: evolving to meet the moment for our customers.

In a recent development, let me be unequivocal: this is not about leaving Docker’s legacy or heritage behind. We’ve spent more than a decade earning your trust. This is about building on that foundation, not replacing it.

According to recent reports, the qualities you value us for aren’t changing. We’re still committed to openness and industry collaboration. We’re still, and always will be, developer-first. We’re still fanatical about simplicity, and about showing up everywhere you need us.

Industry observers note that on the product front, the containers you know and love aren’t going anywhere. Containers still play a huge role in the software development lifecycle. As long as that’s the case, Docker will continue leading the way.

It has been revealed that agents have introduced a newly introduced problem. Containers isolate workloads. But agents aren’t workloads. Agents are actors.

Agents make their own decisions about what to run, what to access, and what to change. Developers and enterprises need solutions built specifically to isolate and govern them, so they can give those agents real autonomy without giving up control.

Docker’s next chapter is about delivering exactly that: security, isolation, and governance, so we can all trust agents to do meaningful work without feeling like we’re always one step from catastrophe.

In case I haven’t made it blindingly obvious yet, the new Docker is all about trust.

Recent findings suggest that trust Docker because our track record speaks for itself. Trust Docker because we’re proven, neutral, and secure. Trust Docker because it’s pretty darn clear you can’t trust the agents to manage themselves.

Industry observers note that trust us because we have a software supply chain that is already the standard for building securely. Trust us because nobody isolates agents where they run better than we do. Trust us because we’re taking a comprehensive approach to improving governance and minimizing risk across the entire enterprise.

Trust Docker because we’re not egotistical enough to think we can solve a challenge this substantial alone. Trust us because everything about our history, our heritage, and our actions over the past year tells you we’ll partner with the smartest and build alongside the best, and not create vendor lock-in.

Most of all, trust Docker because we’re not just talking the talk. We’ve got the goods to back it up: trusted supply chain for your agents to build from, trusted runtime to isolate your agents, and a trusted ecosystem to ensure all the layers of trust are covered, whether made by Docker or not.

According to recent reports, as our product team innovated to meet the moment and our messaging in the market began to shift, one thing became clear: the speed and scale of evolution happening inside Docker called for an equally momentous evolution on the outside. Something that makes it unmistakably clear that it’s a newly introduced day for Docker. Something that says and indicates, loud and clear, for all the world to see, that Docker is not just about containers anymore.

Something, dare I say, whale sized.

I’m talking, of course, about our beloved Moby.

If you know Docker, then you know Moby, and if Docker is evolving, Moby should too. The only question was to how and to what extent? We looked at a lot of whales, folks. (I may or may not have been seeing whales in my sleep.) Ultimately, with the help of our friends at the strategic brand transformation company, Motto, we landed on a newly introduced Moby for the new Docker.

Watch Moby’s transformation here:.

Sources indicate that in many ways, Moby is a microcosm for Docker and the changes we’re making: the Moby you love and trust, evolved for a new era. Just as the new Docker is no longer singularly defined by containers, neither is the new Moby.

We’ve got lots to show you. Poke around our latest website. Find and engage with the new Docker brand on social media. And if you want to see what trust in the agentic era looks like in practice, try Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance. We’d love to hear what you think.

Wherever this new era takes us, Docker will always honor and cherish the trust you continue to place in us. Now, let’s go build what’s next.

Chief Marketing Officer, Docker.

Terri Avnaim is the CMO of Docker, where she leads global marketing and shapes the organization’s positioning and go-to-market strategy for the agentic era.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, openJDK and Oracle disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) on November 17, and NGINX released fixes for two HTTP/2 flaws the next day. Docker began publishing fixed images for both in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog starting that same day.

Sources indicate that what we know about Java4Shell is that it’s a memory-corruption bug in the Java runtime that can let an attacker with no credentials run code inside a Java application. Many container images contain a Java runtime, including application images that bundle their own, so it affects teams well beyond the ones that write Java.

Recent findings suggest that docker Hardened Images are the trusted foundation your applications should run on, because a flaw in the runtime inside an image is fixed only when that image is rebuilt, and Docker rebuilds its hardened images as soon as upstream fixes become available. Fixed images for the Amazon Corretto, SapMachine and Azul Zulu runtimes and for NGINX are in the catalog today, with Eclipse Temurin following as soon as Adoptium completes its fixed builds.

According to recent reports, to decode Base64 swiftly, the HotSpot JVM uses a hand-written routine built on AVX-512 instructions. That routine miscalculates a length when the input ends in unexpected padding and writes up to 62 bytes past the end of a buffer on the Java heap. Calif, the researchers who found it, turned that into heap disclosure and remote code execution.

They demonstrated code execution before authentication against default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and after authentication against Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. They note there is no universal exploit: each application needs its own, and they have not published those. As of November 18 there are no public reports of exploitation in the wild.

Oracle rates the problem 8.1 (High) under CVSS 3.1. The researchers rate it 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0. CISA has issued an alert urging immediate patching.

All three of these must be true.

Recent findings suggest that to check a host’s CPU, run this on the host or Kubernetes node. Hardened runtime images have no shell, so it will not run inside the container.

grep -m1 ‘^flags’ /proc/cpuinfo | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep -E ‘^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$’.

The host is affected if all four flags are printed.

Two other ways to check, for when a shell on the node is hard to get.

It has been revealed that ask the JVM. This works in hardened images:.

docker run –rm –entrypoint java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -w UseAVX.

Sources indicate that useAVX = 3 means the JVM is using AVX-512 on that host. Treat the host as affected until the full check indicates otherwise. A value of 0 to 2 means AVX-512 is not in use. On ARM64 nothing is printed. The answer applies only to the host the command ran on.

Recent findings suggest that ask Kubernetes. kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type demonstrates the architecture and instance type of every node. If you run Node Feature Discovery, nodes with the instruction set carry the label feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-cpuid.AVX512VBMI=true.

It has been revealed that check build runners and CI workers as well. They run Java, and they talk to the network.

docker run –rm –entrypoint java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -w UseAVX.

UseAVX = 3 means the JVM is using AVX-512 on that host. Treat the host as affected until the full check says otherwise. A value of 0 to 2 means AVX-512 is not in use. On ARM64 nothing is printed. The answer applies only to the host the command ran on.

In a recent development, ask Kubernetes. kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type shows the architecture and instance type of every node. If you run Node Feature Discovery, nodes with the instruction set carry the label feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-cpuid.AVX512VBMI=true.

In a recent development, check build runners and CI workers as well. They run Java, and they talk to the network.

Fixed. The published Zulu images we checked report 17.0.21.1+2, 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2 and 27.0.1.1+4.

According to recent reports, waiting for Adoptium to complete its release. On November 18 Adoptium had published 27.0.1.1+4 for x86-64 Linux only. 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1 and 25.0.5.1 were still in testing. Adoptium tracks progress in adoptium/temurin#326. Our published images still report 17.0.21+9, 21.0.13+9, 25.0.5+8 and 27.0.1.0.2+1, which are vulnerable.

Java 26 reached end of support in September 2026, so no fix is expected from any vendor, and it is not among the fixed lines in the OpenJDK advisory. If you run it, treat it as affected and keep the flag set. We recommend moving to Java 25 or updating to Java 27. If you cannot migrate yet, ask us whether Extended Lifecycle Support can cover your version. It is the Docker Hardened Images Enterprise add-on for software past its upstream end of life.

Sources indicate that not affected by this CVE and no action is needed for it. The same November enhancement fixes other issues in these lines, so update when upcoming images arrive.

Application images that bundle Java, such as Keycloak, Jenkins, Kafka, Elasticsearch and Solr.

Industry observers note that they follow the bundled runtime, which for many of them is Temurin, and they are rebuilt once the runtime they use is fixed. Until then, set the flag yourself.

Industry observers note that set the mitigation flag yourself on every JVM that is still waiting for a fixed runtime, and check what each image already sets before you do. Treat the flag as a stopgap, because a JVM is protected only if the flag reaches it when it starts, and a deployment setting or a start script can override it or drop it. A fixed runtime is the only thing that closes the problem, so move to the fixed image as soon as it is published.

It has been revealed that the CPU check and the mitigation flag in the steps below apply to any image that runs a HotSpot-based OpenJDK build. The version strings in this post come from Docker Hardened Images, so for an image from another source, confirm the fixed build in that source’s advisory.

The fixed build can only come from whoever builds your image, because the Java runtime and the system packages your application runs on come from the image underneath it. That dependency is why a hardened image is a necessary step toward a trusted software supply chain. With Docker Hardened Images, tracking each vendor’s fix and rebuilding on it is work Docker does for you. The images are minimal and secure by default, and they are built to serve as a trusted and verifiable upstream for your builds. You can move a service onto one by following the migration guide.

Recent findings suggest that A container often runs more than one JVM, for example when a build tool forks a JVM for tests, an application server starts helper processes or a CI agent starts a JVM for every build step. The flag protects only the JVMs that receive it, and the variable most people reach for first is JAVA_OPTS, which Java does not read at all.

Industry observers note that the JVM itself, however it is started. Includes javac, keytool and other JDK tools.

Yes, through the inherited environment.

A Java 8 JVM that sees it refuses to start. Some DHI FIPS images already set this variable.

Only the java launcher, Java 9 and later.

Yes, when the child is started with java.

Not read by javac, keytool or other JDK tools. DHI FIPS images set it. Java 8 ignores it.

Nothing downstream inherits it.

JAVA_OPTS, JENKINS_JAVA_OPTS, MAVEN_OPTS, ES_JAVA_OPTS and similar.

A start script, which copies the value onto one java command line.

Industry observers note that each script has its own rules. If nothing in the image reads the variable, it does nothing.

Five rules follow from that table. We tested each on DHI images.

JAVA_OPTS only works where a script reads it. With JAVA_OPTS=”-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics” set and a plain java command, the intrinsic stays on. No warning is printed.

A flag on the command line stops at that process. We started a JVM with the flag on its command line and had it start a second JVM. The child ran with the intrinsic on. With JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS in the environment, the child ran with it off. A child started with a cleared environment gets nothing, whichever variable you use.

Sources indicate that check what the image already sets before you set anything. In Docker and Kubernetes, your value replaces the image’s value. It is not appended.

docker inspect –format ‘{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}’ \  | grep -E ‘^(JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS|JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS)=’.

Recent findings suggest that our FIPS images use these variables to configure the FIPS provider. dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:21-fips sets both. When we replaced its JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS with only the flag, the JVM started normally, but the org.bouncycastle.fips.approved_only property was gone. Nothing warned us. If the command prints a value, copy it and add the flag at the end:.

env:  – name: JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS    value: “ -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics”.

Not every FIPS image uses the same variables, so run the check for each image.

Sources indicate that keep JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS away from Java 8. Java 8 is not affected and does not know the flag:.

Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -XX:-UseBASE64IntrinsicsUnrecognized VM option ‘UseBASE64Intrinsics’Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.

Adding -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions to the variable does not help on Java 8. Where Java 8 shares an environment with a newer Java, either scope the variable to the containers that need it or use JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS, which Java 8 ignores. Java 11 accepts the flag, so it is harmless there.

Verify the process, not the environment. Running java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version inside a container starts a new JVM. It tells you what the environment gives a new JVM, not what the JVM already serving traffic was started with. For the running process, use the startup log line. JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS prints one too, starting with NOTE: Picked up. In an image that includes the JDK you can also ask the process directly:.

jcmd VM.flags | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics.

Industry observers note that the answer must be -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. If the flag reached the JVM through an environment variable, it will not show in the process’s command line, so ps is not a reliable check.

Some applications discard these variables on purpose. Elasticsearch’s start script, for example, ignores JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and expects ES_JAVA_OPTS. Check your application’s documentation.

It has been revealed that pull the upcoming image and redeploy. Four things catch people out:.

In a recent development, then confirm with java -version that what is running reports a fixed build. After that, remove the flag from every place you set it.

The day after Java4Shell, NGINX released fixes for two memory errors in the way it handles HTTP/2 connections, tracked as CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. A crafted request can crash a worker process, and where an attacker gets past the operating system’s memory protections it can run code inside that worker. Both flaws need HTTP/2 to be enabled on the server, and the same releases fix other NGINX issues that do not depend on HTTP/2, so enhancement either way.

It has been revealed that the Docker Hardened Images for NGINX were rebuilt on NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 and published on November 18, the same day as the upstream release. To patch, pull the image again and redeploy, and move any tag pinned to an older exact version to a fixed one. nginx -v prints the version, and the fixed ones are 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. The notes on pull policy, mirrors and your own images in the section above apply to NGINX images in the same way.

It has been revealed that the vulnerable code is in the Java runtime inside the image, and if you are using DHI, shipping the fix becomes our job. Whether that code can be reached in your deployment depends on things an image cannot see: the CPU it is scheduled onto, the options you start it with, the processes it starts, and the traffic you send it.

With Docker Hardened Images, Docker will.

Track every Java vendor and ship fixed runtimes in DHI as soon as they are released.

Track every Java vendor yourself and rebuild your base images on each fixed runtime.

Tell you which images are fixed and which are still waiting.

Find out from each vendor which of its builds are fixed.

Tell you what we know, and patch this post.

Follow the OpenJDK, Oracle and vendor advisories as they change.

Three jobs stay with you whichever image you run.

It has been revealed that it was only four weeks ago that the news was PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Calif, the security research team that found Java4Shell and helped find PHP2Shell, claims it used AI to find this flaw in about an hour and that the whole effort cost less than $200 in tokens. When a flaw like this can be found and weaponized at that price, it is reasonable to expect more of them.

It has been revealed that if you lead a team or answer for how your organization builds and ships software, the questions after a week like this one are whether you were exposed and how promptly you can prove you were not. It is imperative to have a trusted foundation in place before the next flaw appears, and Docker Hardened Images is that foundation to adopt. This week Docker began publishing fixed Java and NGINX images to the catalog within a day of each disclosure, with the images still waiting listed in the status table above. Each image ships with a signed SBOM and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, so you have a record of what it contains and how it was built.

The Docker Hardened Images catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, and moving one of your services onto a hardened image typically means changing one line in its Dockerfile. If you are not building on Docker Hardened Images yet, start today.

British retailer Next downplays data breach at tech supplier

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Retailer insists customer details are safe and the data accessed is 'benign,' but won't say exactly what hackers got their hands on.
  • British retailer Next has become the latest high street name to find itself caught up in a cyberattack, although it insists the data accessed by hackers is "benign" and its customers have nothing to worry about.
  • In a recent development, the clothing and homeware giant told investors on Monday that a third-party supplier had suffered a security breach, allowing an unauthorized party to access information relating to Next.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Retailer insists customer details are safe and the data accessed is 'benign,' but won't say exactly what hackers got their hands on.

British retailer Next has become the latest high street name to find itself caught up in a cyberattack, although it insists the data accessed by hackers is "benign" and its customers have nothing to worry about.

In a recent development, the clothing and homeware giant told investors on Monday that a third-party supplier had suffered a security breach, allowing an unauthorized party to access information relating to Next. The retailer claims its own systems remain untouched and that, so far, there's no evidence that customer personal data has fallen into the wrong hands.

"We have been informed that one of our third-party online suppliers has experienced a cyber incident which has resulted in unauthorized access to certain benign data relating to NEXT," the organization remarked in its statement, which it shared with The Register. "We took immediate steps to investigate the nature and scope of the incident with the supplier.".

The breached supplier provides technology services to Next, and the "benign" information accessed is understood to be low-level data. Sensitive customer details, including addresses, passwords, and banking information, are believed to be unaffected.

It has been revealed that next hasn't identified the supplier, explained exactly what the hackers managed to get their hands on, or revealed how much information was accessed, and declined to say when asked by The Register. However, the retailer has seemingly decided that the stolen data won’t be of much use to the criminals responsible.

"Our investigations are ongoing; however, current evidence indicates that no customer personal data has been compromised," Next said. "The information affected is limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or NEXT.".

Next also stressed that its own IT infrastructure had escaped unscathed, saying it was "confident that NEXT’s own systems have not been compromised and that this remains an incident affecting the supplier's environment.".

Despite repeatedly describing the compromised information as harmless, Next says it is treating the incident "with the utmost seriousness" and is working with the affected supplier, law enforcement, and relevant regulators.

The incident comes just weeks after fellow British fashion retailer Asos suffered a breach of its own, with hackers gaining access to customer information through third-party platforms.

Industry observers note that that attack, which came to light on October 6 when customers received an unauthorized push notification through the Asos app announcing that the manufacturer had been hacked, was traced to a social engineering scam. An attacker impersonated a trusted contact to trick an Asos employee into handing over login credentials, which were then used to access external platforms.

Asos later admitted that the intruders had accessed customer names, contact details, and some account information, but passwords and payment card details were apparently off limits.

According to recent reports, next reckons its customers have been luckier, but there’s a lot it isn’t telling us. The firm has gone to some lengths to assure customers that the stolen data is harmless, but without knowing what was taken or who was supposed to be looking after it, we're largely left taking its word for it. ®.

#115560. Prove your AI agent guardrails work

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3192 w)

Prove your AI agent guardrails work

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, you ask a coding agent to clean up one repository.
  • It has been revealed that in Sandboxing Claude and MCP, Hrittik walked through running Claude Code and an MCP server inside Docker Sandboxes using its command-line interface, sbx.
  • Recent findings suggest that now extend that workflow to a team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, you ask a coding agent to clean up one repository. If it has broad permissions, it may also reach your home directory, use your development credentials, and send requests to services you never approved. That gap between the task and the access you grant can turn a routine coding session into a data leak or lost work.

It has been revealed that in Sandboxing Claude and MCP, Hrittik walked through running Claude Code and an MCP server inside Docker Sandboxes using its command-line interface, sbx. That walkthrough started with outbound access blocked, allowed the endpoints needed for the task, and inspected requests to other destinations, including telemetry. The useful part was seeing an actual request fail at the network boundary.

Recent findings suggest that now extend that workflow to a team. Models and providers will change, but the access rules still need to hold. A sandbox limits what an agent can reach on one machine. Organization governance adds shared rules, a managed way to run agents, and records of policy decisions. In this post, we’ll look at how one laptop can affect the whole organization, review two reported incidents, and connect them to four Docker controls: network policy, filesystem policy, managed credentials, and MCP access. Then we’ll test the network and filesystem controls with a simple bank administrator demo.

If an agent exposes a developer’s SSH key or cloud token, every system that accepts that credential may need investigation. The security team must work out what left the machine, replace or revoke exposed credentials, and check whether anyone used them. Deleted work can also halt development. Keep backups of work that has not yet reached the repository.

The compliance consequences depend on the data and the organization. A personal data breach can trigger GDPR notification duties, subject to the applicable risk thresholds. HIPAA has separate requirements for covered entities and business associates following breaches of unsecured protected health information. India’s DPDP framework also includes breach duties, but those provisions are scheduled to take effect in May 2027. For a SOC 2 examination, the question is whether the relevant controls operate as described. SOC 2 is not a breach-notification law.

Data sovereignty adds another question: where does the data go, and who controls it? Before approving a model API endpoint, establish where prompts and outputs are processed and stored, who can access them, and which contracts and laws apply. A provider’s nationality alone does not answer those questions. Network policy can restrict the destination, but it cannot prove how the provider handles data after receiving it.

Industry observers note that this gets harder when developers choose and configure agents independently. A rule on one laptop may be missing on the next. An ignore file may stop one component from reading a file while another component includes it in an upload. Written policy needs matching controls in the software that runs the agent.

Industry observers note that in July 2026, developers reported two incidents where a coding agent went far beyond its task. In one, data left the machine. In the other, files were deleted from it.

It has been revealed that in an X post that has since been deleted, a user noted Grok had uploaded their entire user directory, including SSH keys, a password manager database, and personal files. A Hacker News discussion brought wider attention to the claim. The home-directory claim remains the user’s account. The separate investigation below tested repository uploads.

According to recent reports, researcher Cereblab intercepted Grok Build CLI traffic and found a background upload running alongside the coding task. In a test with a 12 GB repository, about 5.1 GiB had left the machine before the capture stopped, and the upload was still running. The data went to Google Cloud Storage. Fake secrets planted in the repository also appeared in the traffic without being hidden. At the time, turning off “Improve the model” did not stop the repository uploads.

In a recent development, in a reproducible follow-up, the researcher rebuilt the repository from a captured Git bundle, an archive of tracked files and Git history. The bundle included files the agent had been told not to read. Telling the model not to read a file didn’t stop the CLI from packaging and uploading it in the background.

Recent findings suggest that there was a subsequent change. The researcher’s updated timeline indicates whole-repository uploading was disabled server-side on July 13 and remained off when retested on July 22.

The fix does not change the lesson. A coding agent is more than the model. It includes the CLI and any background processes, and those can act without the model asking. Give the whole application only the access its task needs. This is the principle of least privilege.

It has been revealed that on July 10, Matt Shumer wrote: “GPT-5.6-Sol just accidentally deleted almost ALL of my Mac’s files.” He shared the agent’s acknowledgment and confirmed that Full Access was enabled. His follow-up described the loss of his home directory.

Recent findings suggest that A separate experiment reveals why blocking one command is a fragile response. Developer LinearUncle reported that, after a plugin blocked rm, the agent tried unlink, find -delete, and apply_patch. A later attempt to move files to Trash through the GUI failed on permissions; a call to Node’s fs.unlink succeeded. The plugin’s own documentation describes it as an additional guardrail and recommends sandboxing and backups.

Industry observers note that the common issue is excessive access. A model can choose a different tool, and a background process can run outside the model’s visible workflow. Filesystem and network boundaries need to constrain both.

Docker Sandboxes runs each agent in a microVM, a lightweight virtual machine with its own Linux kernel and Docker Engine. A workspace mount shares a host directory with the sandbox. A proxy on the host checks outgoing connections against network policy. The isolation documentation explains these boundaries.

That gives a developer a useful starting point. Share the project needed for the task, restrict outbound access, and inspect failures before adding permissions. Unnecessary telemetry endpoints can remain blocked while the required model and package services are allowed.

Recent findings suggest that choose mounts carefully. A writable mount shares real host files, so changes and deletions inside it affect your machine. Check additional mounts too, including shared agent skills where enabled. Docker’s clone mode gives the agent a private copy of a Git repository so you can review its commits before bringing them back. Isolation limits access, but files in a writable host mount still need backups. Clone mode still exposes the host repository for reading, including ignored files. Keep secrets outside it.

According to recent reports, local settings leave a rollout problem. A teammate can choose different rules or run an agent directly on the host. The organization needs a managed way to run agents, a way to require its use, and visibility into which sessions it covers.

The diagram below demonstrates how organization and team policies reach managed sandbox sessions, where access checks occur, and how policy decisions feed audit records.

Sources indicate that figure 1. Organization and team policies govern access for enrolled, licensed sandbox sessions.

According to recent reports, docker AI Governance lets administrators manage sandbox rules and MCP access centrally. MCP, short for Model Context Protocol, connects agents to tools and data sources. Administrators define policies in Docker Home. On developer machines, sandbox mount checks, the host proxy, and Docker’s MCP gateway enforce the relevant rules. This gives teams shared access rules and records they can review when something goes wrong.

In a recent development, network policies allow or deny destinations such as domain names, IP addresses, and IP ranges written in CIDR notation. For a restricted workflow, start with access denied and allow only the destinations the task needs. Under organization governance, local allow rules cannot grant extra access. Deny rules win, and developers can add local network restrictions.

In a recent development, this can block a background upload to an unapproved destination. But an approved hostname may still handle several kinds of traffic. In the Grok investigation, model requests and storage uploads used different URL paths on the same hostname, so a hostname-only allow rule would not distinguish them. Docker AI Governance now supports more granular network policies: on an allowed host, rules can match the HTTP method, URL path, and query parameters. For example, a policy can permit an agent to open a GitHub pull request while blocking requests to merge it. These finer-grained rules complement filesystem restrictions, which limit the data an application can collect and send.

According to recent reports, filesystem policies control which host paths may be mounted. A writable mount needs both read and write permission; a read-only mount needs read. If a filesystem deny rule and an allow rule match the same request, the deny wins. The decision happens when the sandbox is created. Once a writable mount exists, the agent can modify or delete files within it, regardless of whether it uses rm, a patch tool, or a programming language API.

Recent findings suggest that for proxy-managed credentials, the host proxy adds authentication to outbound requests. The agent can authenticate to an approved service without receiving the raw secret inside the microVM. Credentials can also be scoped to a named sandbox.

Recent findings suggest that this reduces the need to paste API tokens into prompts or store them in the workspace. The protection applies to proxy-managed credentials. A real token placed in an environment variable, a mounted file, or a passthrough login response may still be visible inside the sandbox. Limit what each credential can access and how long it stays valid. Storing a token through the proxy does not change its permissions or expiry.

Sources indicate that MCP access policies govern server registration and subsequent requests through Docker’s MCP gateway. With MCP enforcement active, access requires an explicit permit, and a forbid rule overrides it. Administrators can control tool calls, resource reads, and prompt retrieval, rather than treating an approved server as permission to do everything it offers.

It has been revealed that registration and use are separate decisions. Blocking latest registrations does not stop access to a server that is already registered. Rules checked on each request handle that case. Direct connections to remote MCP servers also need network controls because they bypass Docker’s gateway. Check where each server runs too: local stdio servers run on the host, outside the sandbox VM. Their host access needs separate review.

The next diagram summarizes the four controls to review together: network access, host mounts, managed credentials, and MCP tools.

Industry observers note that figure 2. Network, filesystem, credentials, and MCP controls apply to the whole agent application.

Administrators manage organization and team policies in Docker Home. Group mapping can keep Docker teams in sync with the organization’s identity provider. Policy updates take up to five minutes to reach developer machines. Network changes then apply to fresh requests. Filesystem changes require removing and recreating affected sandboxes because existing mounts keep their original access.

Recent findings suggest that sign-in enforcement is also part of deployment. IT distributes it through endpoint management so developers must authenticate as members of an approved organization. This prevents personal-account bypass within sbx. Your endpoint controls also need to cover agents launched outside that managed workflow.

It has been revealed that suppose you are a bank administrator. Developers want to use coding agents, and you need to enforce the bank’s access rules. Let’s keep the demo to two simple requirements:.

Sources indicate that we’ll use fictional logs and a shell sandbox to check both boundaries without needing a model API. The results below describe what to expect when you run the demo.

Recent findings suggest that install sbx on macOS or Linux and sign in with an AI Governance licensed test user. You’ll also need permission to manage policies and audit delivery in a test organization:.

Run these commands in your host terminal to create a workspace and a separate directory containing a fictional bank log:.

In a recent development, next, enable AI Governance for your organization. In Docker Home, open AI Platform → Manage and turn on AI Governance:.

Figure 3. Enable AI Governance in Docker Home before configuring organization policies.

Next, create the bank’s network and filesystem access rules.

Recent findings suggest that first, let’s look at network access. In a bank, you don’t want employees’ coding agents connecting to just any website. For this demo, we’ll allow the sandbox to reach only hrittikhere.com (standing in for the bank’s website) over HTTPS.

Once AI Governance is enabled, open AI Platform → Network access → Create policy and enter the following values:.

With this as the only applicable network allow rule, all other destinations remain blocked by default.

In a recent development, the curl checks below request headers without following redirects, so they need only hrittikhere.com:443. If you later add -L to follow a redirect to www.hrittikhere.com, allow that exact hostname on port 443 as well.

In a recent development, next, let’s protect the bank’s logs. Employees may need a coding agent to work on a project, but that agent should not be able to read or modify sensitive logs in the home directory. We’ll allow access to the demo workspace and block access to bank-logs.

Open AI Platform → Filesystem access → Create policy.

Note: Use ~ in policy paths, not $HOME; environment variables are not expanded by the policy engine.

According to recent reports, first, allow the project workspace with the values below. A writable workspace needs both Read and Write permissions for sandbox creation to succeed:.

~/sbx-bank-demo/workspace~/sbx-bank-demo/workspace/**.

In the same bank-demo-filesystem policy, add a second rule named bank-demo-logs to deny access to the protected logs:.

~/sbx-bank-demo/bank-logs~/sbx-bank-demo/bank-logs/**.

The workspace allow rule covers workspace and its descendants; it does not include the sibling bank-logs directory. The logs are protected by the explicit deny rule.

It has been revealed that save the policies. You can also check their rules and scope in the Platform UI. Allow up to five minutes for policy sync, then inspect the active rules:.

Figure 6. Active organization rules allow hrittikhere.com:443 and the workspace, and deny bank-logs mounts.

Create a fresh sandbox with only the approved workspace:.

From the host terminal, run the following requests inside the sandbox. The –max-time 15 option caps each request at 15 seconds, so a stalled request times out instead of hanging:.

The first request should return HTTP headers from the approved site:.

Figure 7. The approved HTTPS request to hrittikhere.com returns HTTP 200.

According to recent reports, figure 8. The request to example.com returns HTTP 403; the network log confirms the policy decision.

You can also check the network log to confirm that the failure came from policy enforcement:.

The network log distinguishes allowed traffic from requests blocked by policy:.

Figure 9. The network log records hrittikhere.com:443 as allowed and example.com:443 as blocked.

Sources indicate that run both commands below from your host terminal so $HOME expands to the same host path. First read the fictional log on the host, then request that path inside the sandbox:.

Recent findings suggest that figure 10. The host can read the fictional bank log.

Recent findings suggest that the sandbox command should fail with “No such file or directory” because bank-logs is not mounted. This checks filesystem isolation; the next command tests mount-policy enforcement:.

It has been revealed that figure 11. The unmounted bank-logs path returns “No such file or directory” inside the sandbox.

Now check whether a developer could add the logs as a read-only mount:.

Creation should fail with a mount policy denied error:.

Figure 12. The bank-demo-logs rule rejects the read-only mount with a Read policy denial.

A read-only mount still requires Read permission. The bank-demo-logs rule denies Read, so :ro does not bypass the policy.

You can also review the policy decisions in the Docker Home UI under AI Platform → Audit logs → Audit events. Filter by the test user and time, then inspect the denied mount request for bank-logs. Look for filesystem_mount, the deny decision, the resource path, and the user. If Cloud delivery was disabled during the test, enable it and repeat the mount request.

Figure 13. Audit events record the denied bank-logs mount and allowed workspace mounts.

According to recent reports, these audit records capture governance decisions, not every file operation or the agent’s prompts and output. sbx policy log indicates network traffic; use the audit view for the mount decision. Docker also supports local JSONL audit files and Cloud delivery for hosted search, CSV export, and SIEM forwarding.

The bank now has a simple access-control check: the approved site is reachable, an unapproved site is blocked, and protected logs cannot be read or mounted. This supports the bank’s compliance work; it does not establish compliance on its own.

After reviewing the results, remove the sandbox:.

You can then remove the fictional demo files and the test policies.

Putting AI governance policies in place is only the first step. The real challenge is making sure those policies are practical, consistently enforced, and easy to verify as more developers start using coding agents. A few good practices can help teams reduce unnecessary access, apply the right restrictions to different workloads, and maintain visibility into what agents are doing. Here are five recommendations to keep in mind when rolling out Docker AI Governance across your organization:.

In a recent development, the same questions apply when agents run in continuous integration (CI) jobs or other environments: which host files can they access, which services can they reach, and which credentials can they use? Check which controls each environment supports and repeat the tests there. A policy on a developer’s laptop does not automatically protect an unrelated container or production cluster.

Sources indicate that for security teams, useful evidence connects a licensed, signed-in user to an active policy, a blocked action, and a record they can find. Check sign-in enforcement and license coverage alongside policy. An empty audit dashboard may mean some sessions were never covered.

In a recent development, sandboxing limits an agent’s access on one machine. Governance applies shared rules to managed sessions across the organization. Providers will fix individual failures, but the next failure may look different. Limit which files, services, and credentials it can affect, then test those limits and check the records.

Start with the local sandboxing walkthrough, inspect your rules with sbx policy ls, and run the bank demo with your platform or security team. Use the Docker AI Governance documentation and announcement to plan a small rollout. Expand it after you have checked both the blocked actions and the audit records.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • July bug overwhelmed newer servers, prompting promises of stronger safeguards and faster recovery.
  • Some emails never reached their recipients during November's Microsoft 365 outage, the organization has confirmed in a final report that also exposes gaps in its testing and recovery procedures.
  • According to recent reports, the post-incident report details how a Windows defect brought down Exchange Online and disrupted features across other Microsoft 365 services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

July bug overwhelmed newer servers, prompting promises of stronger safeguards and faster recovery.

Some emails never reached their recipients during November's Microsoft 365 outage, the organization has confirmed in a final report that also exposes gaps in its testing and recovery procedures.

According to recent reports, the post-incident report details how a Windows defect brought down Exchange Online and disrupted features across other Microsoft 365 services. For affected users, the cloud became someone else's unavailable computer.

Recent findings suggest that A preliminary report had already blamed a July code change, combined with a failover and reduced capacity. The final report confirms those findings and sets out Microsoft's intends to improve change auditing and recovery procedures, and add spare capacity. The defect affected Microsoft's gateway server configuration, not standard Windows deployments.

The epic outage (named the "Microsoft long weekend" by some wags) kicked off on November 12 and wasn't fully resolved until November 14.

Microsoft extended its delivery retry window to 48 hours, but some delayed messages destined for consumer mailboxes inactive for more than 30 days still expired, generating non-delivery reports. The company mentioned all queued enterprise messages were eventually delivered, with none found permanently lost.

The report is grim, particularly in how the failure ramped up as US owners came online to find gateway servers toppling over. At the worst point, more than 80 percent of North American gateway servers were unresponsive.

The problem proved elusive, and it took Microsoft some time to identify the change and deploy a fix.

It has been revealed that microsoft has had a week to ponder what it did and did not do, and the report has some next steps to avoid a repeat of November's events. Some are obvious, and some are a little surprising.

It has been revealed that working to reduce the blast radius of failures is an obvious one, and actions include partitioning and isolation to ensure failures can be contained before taking down traffic globally. Recovery procedures also need improvement, along with communication and capacity to ensure there is sufficient headroom.

Microsoft's load tests used older, lower-core-count hardware, making them less likely to expose a defect that worsened on newer machines. The company now plans to test newer hardware with more realistic traffic and peak loads, and broaden its failover testing.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft also plans to improve diagnostics and change auditing so engineers can identify troublesome Windows changes faster. July's defect had been running worldwide for more than three months before it brought the gateways down. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Minister claims intruders downloaded more than 130 GB of data as political churn left security neglected.

The Ancient Thracian heartland of Bulgaria says it has shut down a cyberespionage operation that gave intruders access to government networks for five years – the longest-running known campaign against its administration.

Bulgaria's Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation noted the unauthorized and officially unattributed attackers first gained access to infrastructure used by government institutions to exchange information in 2021.

It explained that the intrusion went unnoticed for so long because "the previous means of protection did not work as a single, integrated system," and that without a fresh, recently installed product, it may have gone undetected for much longer.

"The incident was discovered thanks to the fresh national cybersecurity system, which for the first time provides a single picture of what is happening in state networks," the ministry added.

"Without it, this activity would most likely have remained hidden for an indefinite period of time.".

Bulgaria acknowledged that "sensitive information related to the work of the state" was accessed, but did not specify the scale of the compromise.

It has been revealed that innovation and Digital Transformation Minister Ivan Vasilev stated attackers had downloaded more than 130 GB of data over five years. He also put the volume at 62 million pages.

The Register contacted the Bulgarian government for confirmation of these numbers.

The ministry mentioned that it has not yet found any evidence that citizens' personal data was compromised, and that the affected infrastructure "will be under increased surveillance for 90 days" in case the attackers try to regain access.

Recent findings suggest that vasilev said multiple international hacking groups had accessed government systems since 2021. He did not specify the names of these groups, however, nor did he name any specific countries that may have been involved.

In a follow-up interview with bTV, Vasilev blamed political instability and frequent changes of ministerial leadership for leaving government systems inadequately protected.

A representative of the Progressive Bulgaria party, which back in May won Bulgaria's eighth general election in five years, Vasilev stated the "constant change of leadership" means "important things for the state do not actually happen.".

Industry observers note that vasilev said the intrusion was discovered over the summer as the national cybersecurity system was upgraded, and that teams had spent the past three to four months removing the attackers. ®.
